NOTICE
Notice is hereby given that the Twenty Eighth (28th) Annual General Meeting (“the AGM / 28th AGM”) of the Members of IRB 
Infrastructure Developers Limited (“the Company”) will be held on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, at 11:30 am (IST) through 
Video Conferencing (“VC”) / Other Audio Visual Means (“OAVM”) to transact the following business:
ORDINARY BUSINESS
1.	
To consider and adopt the Audited Consolidated Financial Statements for the financial year ended March 31, 2026, 
together with the Report of the Auditors thereon.
2.	
To consider and adopt the Audited Standalone Financial Statements for the financial year ended March 31, 2026, together 
with the Reports of the Board of Directors and the Auditors thereon.
3.	
To appoint a director in place of Mr. Ravindra Dhariwal (DIN: 00003922), Non-Executive Director who retires by rotation and, 
being eligible, seeks re-appointment and for that purpose to pass with or without modification(s) the following resolution, 
as a Special Resolution:
	
“RESOLVED THAT pursuant to the provisions of Section 152 of the Companies Act, 2013 and the rules related thereto read 
with Regulation 17(1A) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 (including any statutory modification(s) / amendment(s)/ reenactment(s) thereto), Mr. Ravindra Dhariwal 
(DIN: 00003922) who retires by rotation at this meeting and being eligible, offers himself for reappointment and who will 
attain the age of 75 (seventy five) years in September 2027, be and is hereby re-appointed as a Director of the Company 
(Non-Executive, Non-Independent), liable to retire by rotation.”
SPECIAL BUSINESS
4.	
To consider and, if thought fit, to pass with or without modification(s), the following resolution as an Ordinary Resolution:
	
“RESOLVED THAT pursuant to the provisions of Section 148(3) and other applicable provisions, if any, of the Companies 
Act, 2013 read with the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 (including any statutory modification(s) or re-
enactment(s) thereof, for the time being in force), the remuneration payable to Joshi Apte & Associates, Practicing Cost 
Accountant having Firm Registration No. 00240 appointed by the Board of Directors of the Company to conduct the audit 
of the cost records of the Company for the financial year 2026-27, amounting to ` 3,00,000/- (Rupees Three lakh only) 
p.a. plus applicable taxes and reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses at actuals, if any, incurred in connection with the 
audit, be and is hereby ratified and confirmed.
	
RESOLVED FURTHER THAT the Board of Directors or Key Managerial Personnel of the Company be and are hereby 
authorised to do all acts, deed and things, proper or desirable to give effect to this Resolution.”
By Order of the Board of Directors

Date of Birth and Age

Date of first appointment on

Mr. Ravindra Dhariwal was first appointed to the Board on August 05, 2022, as the 
nominee of Cintra INR Investments B.V.
Qualification
An engineer from IIT Kanpur, and an MBA from IIM Calcutta. He was bestowed the 
distinguished Alumni Award by IIM Calcutta in 2013 and also from IIT Kanpur in 2019.
Brief resume & nature of expertise 
in specific functional areas
Mr. Ravindra Dhariwal is the Co-founder and Chairman of Sagacito Technologies, a data 
analytics company focused on enabling enterprises to unlock growth opportunities and 
maximise their revenues through advance insights and analytics. He also serves as a 
Senior Advisor, Mentor and Board Member of several leading listed and private companies.
Prior to co – founding Sagacito Technologies, Mr. Dhariwal served as the Group CEO 
of Bennett, Coleman & Co. Limited, India’s largest media conglomerate, with diversified 
media platforms including the Economic Times, Radio Mirchi, Times Television Network, 
Times Internet, Times Out-of-Home (OOH) and The Times of India, the world’s largest 
circulated English-language newspaper.
Mr. Dhariwal has also contributed significantly to the global media industry. He served as 
the World-Wide President of International News Media Association from 2011-2013. In 
2014 he was honoured for his outstanding voluntary contribution to World News Media 
sector worldwide.
Prior to joining Bennett, Coleman & Co. Limited, Mr. Dhariwal spent 12 years with PepsiCo, 
where he was the Pepsi’s first employee in India and played pivotal role in launching 
Pepsi brands in India. He was instrumental in building PepsiCo’s beverage business and 
subsequently held leadership responsibilities across India, Africa, and Southeast Asia.
Mr. Dhariwal began his professional journey with Unilever in India in 1977 where 
he worked in India and Australia for over 12 years mostly in Sales and Marketing 
management positions.
Over a distinguished career spanning over more than four and half decade, Mr. Dhariwal 
has built and scaled consumer businesses all over the world. His extensive international 
experience, combined with his deep understanding of diverse markets and cultures, 
has enabled organizations to strengthen customer loyalty, enhance brand equity, and 
achieve sustained business growth.

Item No.3
Mr. Ravindra Dhariwal (DIN: 00003922) age 74 years (seventy 
four), is the Non-Executive and Non-Independent Director of 
the Company liable to retire by rotation. 
He will attain the age of 75 (seventy-five) years in September 
2027, and the continuation of his Directorship will be subject 
to approval by the shareholders by way of a special resolution 
as per Regulation 17(1A) of the Listing Regulations. Hence 
the approval of the Members is sought for the continuation 
of his Directorship on the Board of the Company even after 
attaining the age of 75 (seventy-five) years.
Mr. Ravindra Dhariwal is the Co-founder and Chairman of 
Sagacito Technologies, a data analytics company that helps 
enterprises drive growth through advanced insights and 
analytics. A seasoned business leader with over four and 
a half decades of global experience, he has held several 
distinguished leadership roles, including Group CEO of 
Bennett, Coleman & Co. Ltd. (The Times Group), India’s largest 
media conglomerate, and was the Worldwide President of 
the International News Media Association from 2011 to 2013. 
Prior to The Times Group, he spent 12 years with PepsiCo as 
its first employee in India, playing a key role in launching and 
expanding the company’s beverage business across India, 
Africa, and Southeast Asia. He began his career with Unilever 
in 1977, serving in sales and marketing leadership positions in 
India and Australia. Mr. Dhariwal currently serves as a senior 
advisor, mentor, and board member to several leading listed 
and private companies, leveraging his extensive international 
experience to help organizations strengthen brands, build 
customer loyalty, and achieve sustainable growth.
Mr. Dhariwal has participated actively in the deliberations of 
the Board and has provided strategic inputs and guidance 
on matters placed before the Board. During the financial 
year 2025-26, he has attended 10 out of 10 meetings of 
the Board and also attended Annual General Meeting 
as well as Extra Ordinary Meetings. His attendance and 
participation demonstrate his commitment to discharging his 
responsibilities as a director diligently.
The Board considers his experience in Business leadership, 
Business Development, Consumer and Customer insights, 
Corporate Governance, Risk Management, technology 
and data-led business opportunities to be relevant to the 
Company’s business. Given the scale and complexity of 
the Company’s infrastructure business and considering his 
vast leadership experience, deep industry expertise, and 
valuable contributions as a member of the Board, the Board 
is of the view that his continued association will be beneficial 
to the Company.
The Board, including all the members of the Nomination and 
Remuneration Committee, considered and approved the 
proposal for continuation of his directorship beyond the age 
of 75 years and recommends the resolution set out at item 
No. 3 for the approval of the members.
The details required under Regulation 36(3) of the Listing 
Regulations and Secretarial Standards on General Meetings 
(SS-2) issued by the Institute of Company Secretaries of India,

NOTES
1.	
Explanatory Statement pursuant to Section 102 read with 
Section 110 of the Companies Act, 2013 (the “Act”) and 
the Rule 20 and Rule 22 of the Companies (Management 
and Administration) Rules, 2014, as amended, setting 
out material facts relating to the resolutions proposed 
to be passed is annexed hereto.
2.	
The Ministry of Corporate Affairs (‘MCA’), vide its General 
Circular No. 03/2025 dated September 22, 2025, (in 
continuation with the Circulars issued earlier in this 
regard) (‘MCA Circulars’), has allowed the Companies 
to conduct the Annual General Meeting (AGM) through 
Video Conferencing or Other Audio-Visual Means (‘VC/
OAVM’) without the physical presence of Members. In 
compliance with the provisions of the Companies Act, 
2013 (“Act”), SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure 
Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“Listing Regulations”) 
and MCA Circulars, the AGM of the Company is being 
held through VC/OAVM.
3.	
The Company has enabled the Members to participate 
at the AGM through the VC/OAVM facility provided by 
KFin Technologies Limited, Registrar and Share Transfer 
Agents (“KFintech / RTA”). The Members can join the 
AGM in the VC/OAVM mode 15 minutes before the 
scheduled time of the commencement of the Meeting. 
The instructions for participation by Members are given 
in the subsequent pages. Participation at the AGM 
through VC shall be allowed on a first-come-first-served 
basis for first 1,000 members. This will not include 
large Members (Members holding 2% or more equity 
shares), Promoters, Institutional Investors, Directors, 
Key Managerial Personnel, the Chairpersons of the 
Audit Committee, Stakeholders Relationship Committee, 
Auditors etc. who are allowed to attend the AGM without 
restriction on account of first-come-first-served basis. 
The members can visit https://emeetings.kfintech.com 
and login through existing user id and password to 
attend the live proceedings of the AGM of the Company.
4.	
Members may note that pursuant to the provisions of MCA 
and SEBI Circulars, the Annual report for the financial 
year 2025-26 and AGM Notice (including remote e-voting 
instructions) is being sent to Members electronically. 
Accordingly, the Annual Report for the financial year 
2025-26 and AGM Notice are being sent only to those 
members whose names appear in the Register of 
Members / List of Beneficial Owners as on August 21, 
2026, received from the Depositories and whose e-mail 
addresses are registered with the Company or with the 
depository participant / depository. Members may note 
that the Annual Report for the financial year 2025-26 
and AGM Notice will also be available on the Company’s 
website at www.irb.co.in, websites of Stock Exchange(s) 
i.e. BSE Limited and National Stock Exchange of India 
Limited at www.bseindia.com and www.nseindia.com 
respectively and on the website of KFintech at https://
evoting.kfintech.com/.
5.	
As per the Circulars mentioned above, the Members may 
also note that the Company would not be sending the 
Annual Report for the financial year 2025-26 and AGM 
notice by post to the Members whose e-mail address 
is not registered with the Company or depository 
participants/depository.
6.	
The Company is providing a facility to the members 
as on the cut-off date, being Tuesday, September 15, 
2026 (“the cut-off date”) to exercise their right to vote 
on the matters listed in the Notice by electronic voting 
systems (Remote e-voting). Additionally, the members 
can also exercise their right to vote by e-voting during 
the AGM. The process and manner of remote e-voting 
with necessary User ID and password is given below. 
Such remote e-voting facility is in addition to voting that 
will take place at the AGM being held through VC/OAVM. 
Any person who acquires shares of the Company and 
becomes a Member of the company after the dispatch 
of the Notice, and holding shares as on the cut-off date, 
may obtain the User ID and Password by sending a 
request at evoting@kfintech.com or contact KFintech at 
toll free number 1-800-309-4001. Voting by electronic 
mode is a convenient means of exercising voting rights 
and may help to increase the member’s participation in 
the decision-making process.
7.	
The Members who have cast their vote prior to the 
meeting by remote e-voting may also attend the AGM 
but shall not be entitled to vote again. Once a vote is 
cast by a member, he / she shall not be allowed to alter 
it subsequently. In case a Member casts his / her vote, 
both by Remote e-Voting and e-voting at the AGM mode, 
then the voting done by Remote e-Voting shall prevail 
and the e-voting at the AGM shall be invalid.
8.	
Pursuant to the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, 
a Member, entitled to attend and vote at the AGM, is 
entitled to appoint a proxy to attend and vote on his/
her behalf and the proxy need not be a Member of the 
Company. Since this AGM is being held through VC, 
physical attendance of Members has been dispensed 
with. Accordingly, the facility for appointment of proxies 
by the Members will not be available for the AGM and 
hence the Proxy Form, Attendance Slip and Route Map 
are not annexed to this Notice.
9.

the quorum of the meeting under Section 103 of the Act.

About the Report
Understanding our Integrated Reporting Approach
This Integrated Report reflects our commitment to transparent, 
balanced and integrated communication with stakeholders. 
Prepared in alignment with the International Integrated 
Reporting Framework, the Report explains how we create value 
through our strategy, governance, business model, performance 
and outlook across the short, medium and long term.
As one of India’s leading transport infrastructure developers, 
we operate at the intersection of economic development, 
connectivity and sustainable infrastructure. Our integrated 
reporting approach reflects how value is created through the 
dynamic management, optimisation and redeployment of 
infrastructure assets across their lifecycle. Through integrated 
thinking and disciplined capital allocation, we seek to create 
enduring value for all stakeholders while supporting India’s 
infrastructure development aspirations.

Reporting Scope and Boundary
This Report comprises qualitative and quantitative information 
relating to the performance of IRB Infrastructure Developers 
Limited for the reporting period from April 1, 2025, to March 
31, 2026, covering FY 2025-26. We have provided the list of 
subsidiaries, associate companies, and joint ventures that can 
be found in AOC 1 on page no. 448 of this Report.
The environmental, social and governance disclosures 
presented in this Report primarily cover our construction, tolling, 
operations and maintenance activities across our portfolio of 
BOT, TOT and HAM projects in India. Unless otherwise stated, 
the disclosures pertain to operations under our management 
and operational control. 
Responsibility
The Board of Directors and senior management believe 
that this Integrated Report presents a balanced view of 
our strategy, governance, performance and outlook. It 
reflects our commitment to transparency, accountability 
and long-term value creation.
Integrated Thinking and Materiality
The material matters presented in this Report have been 
identified through a structured materiality assessment 
process involving key stakeholder groups and 
management representatives. Stakeholder perspectives 
obtained through structured engagement processes 
have informed the identification of material matters and 
strategic priorities.
The assessment considers the significance of economic, 
environmental, social and governance issues and their 
potential influence on our ability to create long-term 
value. These material matters are integrated into strategic 
planning, enterprise risk management and performance 
monitoring processes.
The Report also reflects our commitment to integrated 
thinking. We seek to strengthen decision-making and 
organisational resilience by fostering connectivity 
between business functions, governance structures, risk 
management systems and sustainability priorities in an 
evolving operating environment.

The non-financial information presented in this Report, 
including BRSR Core disclosures, has been independently 
assured by Carbon Check (India) Private Ltd. Details of the 
assurance can be found on pages 248-254 of this Report.

Stakeholder feedback is integral to our continuous 
improvement process. We actively seek and value inputs

Chairman and MD’s Message
Dear Stakeholders,
Twenty-eight years ago, IRB set out with a single ambition: to build and 
operate world-class road infrastructure for India. FY 2025-26 is the year 
that ambition came of age. If I were to describe it in one word, it would 
be Transformative – not as a description of a single good year, but as the 
culmination of a strategy conceived, tested and refined over two and a 
half decades.
Our B.E.S.T. strategy – Bid, Execute, Stabilise and Transfer 
– is not a slogan we adopted this year; it is the distilled 
wisdom acquired through years of building, owning and 
operating highways across India. In FY 2025-26, that 
wisdom translated into decisive, tangible value creation 
and firmly established IRB as India’s foremost disciplined 
capital-recycling infrastructure platform – a position we 
set out deliberately to earn, and one that is now genuinely 
difficult to replicate.
It is a matter of real satisfaction that this disciplined 
approach has built one of India’s leading, and the largest, 
highway infrastructure asset platforms. Today, the 
IRB Group commands an asset base of approximately 
`94,000 Cr, up from around `80,000 Cr at the start of the 
year. We operate 28 highway assets across 13 states, 
serving millions of road users every day, with our network 
generating over `1 Cr in toll revenue every hour. This did 
not happen by chance – it is the compounding result of a 
platform built asset by asset, cycle by cycle, and it reflects 
the resilience, quality and maturity of a portfolio that stands 
without a true peer in the Indian roads sector.
Yet the true measure of our success extends well beyond 
the numbers. Somewhere on a national highway in India at 
this very moment, a truck is moving seamlessly through a 
toll plaza we developed, a family is travelling on a road we 
operate and maintain, and another digital toll transaction 
is being processed across our network. These everyday 
moments, repeated millions of times, are the quiet but 
powerful proof of the role our infrastructure plays in 
connecting India, facilitating commerce and supporting 
the nation’s economic growth – and they are, for IRB, the 
most meaningful validation of everything this platform 
was built to do.
Our B.E.S.T. 
strategy remains 
the cornerstone of 
our value-creation 
philosophy, and 
FY 2025-26 was the 
year it truly proved 
itself as a capability 
that sets IRB apart.
India continues to be one of the world’s fastest-growing 
major economies. Despite geopolitical uncertainties and 
global economic volatility, the resilience of the Indian 
economy continued to drive growth in both passenger 
mobility and freight movement, reflected in healthy traffic 
growth across our portfolio and stronger toll collections, 
particularly in the second half of the year. This performance 
is an affirmation – of the quality of our assets, the resilience 
of our business model, and the conviction with which we 
have built for India’s long-term infrastructure story.
FY 2025-26 marked another year of strong operational 
execution across our tolling portfolio. Our highways today 
serve nearly 1.5 Mn vehicles every day and account for 
close to 10% of India’s total toll collections. Toll revenue 
across IRB and our Private InvIT platform grew by nearly 
13% year-on-year, driven by healthy traffic growth, periodic 
tariff revisions and the addition of new operational assets.
All major projects are now operational. The capex cycle 
is complete. We enter the next phase from a position of 
strength, with future growth driven by operating leverage, 
rising toll collections, InvIT distributions, asset rotation 
and recurring O&M income.
From Builder to Owner-Operator: A Strategic Coming 
of Age
FY 2025-26 was a defining year – the year our strategic 
transformation was truly completed. Over its operating life, 
IRB consciously and deliberately reshaped its identity from 
a contractor: first into a developer that took on construction 
risk and ownership, and now into a Sponsor and Operations 
& Maintenance-led platform, with a sharp focus on capital 
efficiency, recurring cash flows, long-term annuity income 
and sustainable shareholder returns. Few infrastructure 
companies in India have made this full journey – from 
contractor, to developer, to institutional owner-operator – 
and fewer still have done so while continuing to grow the 
underlying portfolio at the pace we have.
This is more than a change in business mix. It is the 
evolution of IRB from a project development company 
into a platform built on creating, owning, operating and 
monetising high-quality road infrastructure assets at 
scale. It strengthens the resilience of our business model, 
sharpens earnings visibility, and positions us to deliver 
consistent, compounding value for every stakeholder who 
has placed their trust in us.
B.E.S.T.: The Engine Behind an Incomparable 
Platform
Our B.E.S.T. strategy remains the cornerstone of our 
value-creation philosophy, and FY 2025-26 was the year 
it truly proved itself as a capability that sets IRB apart. 
This continuous, disciplined rotation of assets – bidding, 
executing, stabilising and transferring — is the engine 
behind our growth: every rupee of equity is made to work 
multiple times over, rather than being committed once and 
held for decades. It is this capital velocity, built and refined 
over years of execution, that has allowed us to construct 
a portfolio whose scale and quality are, today, genuinely 
difficult for others to match.

We also concluded the transfer of the VM7 (Gandeva–

project to the IRB InvIT Fund, receiving ~`510 Cr towards 
equity investment while consolidated debt reduced by 
approximately `700 Cr – further strengthening our liquidity 
and reaffirming the discipline behind every transfer 
we execute.
As we continue to execute this capital allocation and 
value-creation strategy with conviction, we are steadily 
reducing the Company’s consolidated net debt, with a clear 
objective of achieving a net debt-free position over the 
next five years. This deleveraging trajectory will enhance 
our financial resilience, improve cash return on equity, and 
give us the flexibility to pursue the next phase of growth 
from a position of genuine strength.
A Portfolio that Stands Apart
Although overall project award activity remained relatively 
subdued during the year, IRB Infrastructure Trust continued 
to strengthen its portfolio by securing TOT-17 and TOT-18, 
with an aggregate enterprise value of approximately 
`14,000 Cr – well above our typical annual project 
additions. Once again, we demonstrated the execution 
excellence that has become our hallmark: achieving 
financial closure for TOT-17 within a remarkably short span, 
and successfully commencing tolling operations on TOT-
17 and TOT-18 on January 23, 2026 and April 1, 2026, 
respectively. Collections from both assets have been in line 
with our expectations since commencement, reaffirming our 
confidence in their long-term potential. TOT-17 carries, for 
IRB, a particular significance – connecting some of India’s 
most revered pilgrimage and heritage destinations, and 
enabling safer, faster and more efficient travel for millions of 
commuters and devotees.
With every project across our platform now operational, 
IRB has entered a new phase – one defined by earnings 
stability, operating leverage and long-term revenue 
visibility that few of our peers can claim. The resilience of 
our business model rests on a portfolio in which over 99% 
of our assets are fully constructed and operational, toll 
tariffs are contractually linked to inflation, and operations 
and maintenance costs account for only around 15% of 
our total cost base. These structural advantages give 
us predictable cash flows, resilience across economic 
cycles, and a portfolio quality that clearly and durably 
differentiates IRB from conventional construction-led 
infrastructure companies.
O&M: The Rising Pillar
Our Operations & Maintenance platform is emerging as 
one of the strongest pillars of our future earnings visibility. 
Unlike conventional EPC-led models that depend on 
continuous order-book replenishment, our O&M business 
provides long-duration, annuity-style revenues with stable 
margins and predictable cash flows. Our O&M order 
book alone stands at `428 Bn, offering 15 to 20 years of 
long-term visibility with healthy margins. We expect the 
contribution of O&M revenues to keep increasing steadily, 
further improving the quality, stability and sustainability of 
our earnings profile.
ESG, Governance, and Our Communities
At IRB, sustainability is not a statement – it is a practice 
embedded in every aspect of our operations. Our 
investments in renewable energy solutions, reuse of 
Reclaimed Asphalt Product, eco-engineering techniques 
and low-carbon construction practices underscore this 
commitment, and IRB is rated among the top infrastructure 
companies in India for ESG performance.
Our long-term CSR programmes focus on health, 
education, water conservation and community 
empowerment. Initiatives such as the Sujalam Sufalam 
Schemes reflect our commitment to putting our 
resources to work for social good. We continue to 
maintain robust governance through independent 
boards, comprehensive grievance mechanisms, and ISO 
certifications across quality, environment and occupational 
health (9001, 14001 and 45001).
Pioneering Digital, and Now AI
Innovation has always been integral to IRB’s growth journey. 
We have consistently embraced technology not merely 
to improve efficiency, but to change the way highway 
infrastructure is developed, operated and managed. Over 
the years, IRB has stayed at the forefront of digital adoption 
in the Indian roads sector – we were among the pioneers 
of one of India’s first pilot projects for FASTag-based 
electronic toll collection, and among the first infrastructure 
companies to implement an integrated SAP enterprise 
platform, seamlessly connected with our Toll Management 
System, enabling real-time financial and operational 
reporting across our portfolio.
Today, more than 97% of our toll revenue is collected 
digitally through FASTag, with transactions recorded 
automatically and with no human intervention – 
enhancing operational efficiency, improving transparency, 
strengthening internal controls and delivering a superior 
experience for highway users.
Artificial Intelligence now represents the next frontier of 
this journey. IRB is pleased to share that it has initiated the 
implementation of AI-driven solutions across its Operations 
and Maintenance activities, aimed at enhancing preventive 
maintenance, improving asset monitoring, strengthening 
safety management and enabling more data-driven 
decision-making. While these initiatives are still being 
rolled out, AI, together with advanced analytics and digital 
technologies, is expected to further improve operational 
excellence, enhance customer experience and support 
more efficient lifecycle management of our highway assets 
– adopted, as always, thoughtfully and responsibly, in a 
manner that creates sustainable value for our stakeholders.
Our philosophy remains unchanged: technology is not an 
end in itself – it is an enabler of safer roads, better customer 
service, more efficient operations and stronger long-term 
value creation.
Other Updates
In line with the Company’s Dividend Distribution Policy, we 
declared total dividends of approximately `187 Cr during 
FY 2025-26.
During the year, the Company also received distributions 
of approximately `300 Cr from its two InvIT platforms – a 
clear reflection of the robust and steadily improving cash-
generating ability of our mature operational assets as they 
continue to stabilise and grow.
The Company also completed a 1:1 bonus Issue announced 
during the year, reaffirming our confidence in IRB’s long-
term growth prospects.
The Road Ahead
Following the transfer of three BOT assets from IRB 
Infrastructure Trust and one HAM asset from IRB Infra, the 
Private InvIT has proposed the sale of two BOT highway 
assets, with an enterprise value of approximately `4,605 Cr, 
to the Public InvIT – the B.E.S.T. strategy continuing to do 
exactly what it was built to do. The capital unlocked will be 
redeployed into our next phase of growth.
Building on this momentum, we remain firmly on track to 
expand our road asset portfolio to nearly `1.4 trillion over 
the next three to four years – a target that reflects just how 
far this platform has travelled since IRB’s earliest days as a 
road-building company.
Toll-Operate-Transfer (TOT) projects will continue to be 
our primary growth driver. With the Government’s road 
monetisation pipeline estimated at approximately `4.4 
trillion over the next four to five years – representing 
annual TOT opportunities of `400–500 Bn – IRB is well 
positioned to capitalise on this sizeable opportunity through 
the very capabilities that define us: an integrated platform, 
disciplined capital allocation, and proven expertise in 
acquiring, operating and monetising toll-road assets at a 
scale few in this industry can match.
Gratitude
On behalf of the Board, I extend my sincere appreciation to 
our shareholders for their continued trust and confidence 
– trust that has made this journey from builder to owner-
operator possible. I also thank the National Highways 
Authority of India, MSRDC, HMDA, UPEIDA, our lending 
institutions, investors, business partners and government 
authorities for their continued support and collaboration.
Most importantly, I express my heartfelt gratitude to every 
member of the IRB family. Their commitment, integrity and 
relentless pursuit of excellence have built, brick by brick 
and highway by highway, the platform we stand on today.
As we look ahead, we remain committed to creating 
sustainable long-term value through disciplined 
capital allocation, operational excellence, prudent risk 
management and the highest standards of corporate 
governance. These principles will continue to guide IRB as 
we build infrastructure that contributes to India’s growth, 
while delivering enduring value for our shareholders.

Our ability to deliver large-scale transport infrastructure efficiently and responsibly is anchored 
in strong stakeholder relationships. Continuous engagement helps us understand concerns, 
anticipate expectations and strengthen decision-making across project development, 
construction, operations, maintenance and corporate functions. This collaborative approach 
supports long-term value creation, reinforces our licence to operate and enables us to pursue 
growth opportunities with resilience and accountability.
We maintain structured engagement with our diverse 
stakeholder base, recognising that informed dialogue 
is essential to sound decision-making, operational 
continuity and sustainable value creation. Regular 
interactions and feedback mechanisms help us 
refine priorities, allocate capital effectively and direct 
resources towards areas of strategic, operational and 
societal relevance. Periodic materiality assessments 
further support this process by integrating evolving 
stakeholder expectations into corporate strategy, risk 
management and performance monitoring.
Accountability to stakeholders is embedded in 
our governance philosophy. We cultivate these 
relationships through a clearly-defined engagement 
architecture that reflects each stakeholder’s 
influence, dependency and connection to the 
business. This framework supports differentiated 
engagement across stakeholder groups, strategic 
partners and external influencers, ensuring that 
our interactions remain relevant, inclusive and 
responsive to changing business conditions, 
regulatory developments and project-level realities.
Given the diversity of stakeholder interests, we adopt 
a tailored approach for each stakeholder category, 
calibrated to its role, influence and potential 
impact on business performance and stakeholder 
outcomes. Across all engagements, transparency in 
communication and accountability in action remain 
fundamental. This approach helps us strengthen 
trust, manage risks more effectively, improve service 
delivery and align long-term growth with broader 
stakeholder and societal priorities.

Priorities that Guide our Ascent
Materiality Assessment
A robust materiality assessment guides how we focus our sustainability efforts and report 
transparently on the issues that matter most to stakeholders and long-term value creation. 
Building on previous assessments, we strengthened our approach in FY 2025-26 to reflect both 
our most significant impacts and the ESG issues that are financially material to the business.
Grounded in GRI 3 and informed by leading ESG 
rating methodologies, SASB, IFRS S1/S2 and SEBI’s 
BRSR framework, our double materiality approach 
evaluates environmental, social and governance 
topics through three lenses: stakeholder concerns, 
impact on enterprise value and impact on the 
broader economy, environment and society. This 
helps us connect stakeholder engagement, risk 
management and strategy, while ensuring that our 
disclosures reflect the ESG factors shaping our 
future performance.
Methodology Evolution and Standards 
Alignment
During FY 2025-26, we further evolved materiality 
from a compliance-led exercise into a strategic 
tool that guides how we allocate time, capital and 
management attention. Our enhanced double 
materiality assessment elevated occupational health 
and safety, climate resilience, governance and ethics, 
human capital and responsible supply chains as key 
issues for stakeholders and future performance.
We continued our practice of peer benchmarking and 
sectoral assessment using the SASB Engineering & 
Construction Services Standard. We also aligned the 
process with GRI 3 Material Topics 2021, GRI Universal 
Standards 2021, IFRS S1/S2 guidance and SEBI’s BRSR 
framework. These references ensure that our topic universe 
reflects both impact materiality under GRI and financial 
materiality as viewed by investors and rating agencies.
The key advancement in our methodology is the integration 
of impacts, risks and opportunities into a dynamic double 
materiality framework. Each topic is assessed across 
three dimensions:
	
Stakeholder concerns
	
Impact on the organisation, covering enterprise value
	
Impact on sustainability, covering the economy, 
environment and people
A topic is considered material when it has significant 
actual or potential impacts on people or the environment, 
or when it could reasonably influence the decisions of 
investors and other providers of capital due to its effect 
on enterprise value. Our matrix brings these perspectives 
together and positions each topic based on its importance 
to stakeholders and to the business.
External Frameworks, ESG Rating Methodologies 
and Peer Benchmarking
To complement the GRI 3 impact lens, we mapped 
our topic universe to leading ESG rating providers and 
sector frameworks.
	
ESG Rating Methodologies
We reviewed construction and infrastructure sector 
priorities identified by leading ESG rating providers. 
These include health and safety, human capital 
development, labour management, community relations, 
opportunities in clean technology and water, board 
effectiveness, ownership and control, accounting, 
business ethics and tax transparency. This helped 
confirm the prominence of governance, safety and 
workforce-related topics in our matrix.
	
Materiality Maps and Industry Drivers
Sector materiality maps and industry driver analysis 
emphasise strong corporate governance and 
ethical standards, climate transition and physical 
risk management, sustainable raw materials, waste 
management and advanced human capital management 
in a labour-intensive sector. These references provided a 
useful cross-check for our double materiality positioning 
by assessing both external impact on society and the 
environment and impact on enterprise value creation.

GRI 3 Impact Lens
In line with GRI 3, each potential material topic was 
assessed for positive and negative impacts, with particular 
attention to human rights implications. Negative impacts 
were further categorised as:
	
Caused by the Organisation
Impacts arising directly from our own activities, such 
as safety conditions at construction sites or emissions 
from equipment.
	
Contributed by the Organisation
Impacts where we are not the sole cause, but where 
our decisions or practices influence outcomes, such as 
project timelines or cost structures that may pressure 
contractors’ safety or labour practices.
	
Directly Linked to the Organisation
Impacts caused by value chain partners but linked to us 
through business relationships, such as subcontractor 
labour practices or raw material sourcing impacts.
This analysis supports clearer allocation of responsibility 
and more targeted response strategies, ranging from direct 
remediation where we cause impacts to leverage-based 
engagement across the value chain.
Stakeholder Engagement and Materiality Analysis
Our materiality assessment is closely linked to our 
stakeholder engagement framework. Internal respondents 
representing key stakeholder groups, including investors 
and shareholders, government and authorities, employees, 
suppliers and subcontractors, customers and clients, and 
local communities, participated in the annual materiality 
survey and workshops.
Materiality Matrix and FY 2025-26 Validation
The outcome of this process is a double materiality matrix 
in which each issue is positioned based on its impact on 
stakeholders on the y-axis and its impact on enterprise 
value on the x-axis. The matrix provides a strategic 
overview of our sustainability priorities and highlights 
the issues that require focused management, resource 
allocation and enhanced disclosure.
The matrix is reviewed annually. For FY 2025-26, previously 
identified material topics were reassessed and validated 
using the enhanced approach, incorporating updated 
stakeholder feedback, ERM insights, GRI 3 impact 
categorisation and external references from ESG rating 
providers and peer benchmarking. This exercise confirmed 
the continued relevance of our existing topics, while 
refining their prioritisation and strengthening their linkage 
to strategy and risk management.
Inputs were analysed across three questions:
	
Stakeholder Concerns
What issues matter most to our stakeholders?
	
Impact on the Organisation
How do these issues influence business operations, 
reputation and financial performance?
	
Impact on Sustainability
What are the environmental and social implications 
associated with these issues?
The resulting scores feed into the double materiality matrix, 
with stakeholder concern forming one axis of prioritisation 
alongside impact on enterprise value. Our stakeholder 
saliency framework, covering power, legitimacy, urgency 
and vulnerability, also guides whose inputs carry greater 
weight for specific topics. For example, community inputs 
are especially relevant to road safety and access issues, 
while investor and regulator inputs are critical to governance 
and ethics.
Through this analysis, 13 material issues critical to our 
strategic focus were identified and validated by the ESG 
Committee to ensure alignment with our sustainability goals, 
risk appetite and stakeholder expectations.
Scoring Methodology and ERM Integration
We have integrated our Enterprise Risk Management process 
into the materiality framework to strengthen the robustness 
of our assessment. This enables us to systematically identify 
and evaluate risk factors, emerging trends, impact severity 
and likelihood of occurrence. It also supports targeted ESG 
strategies and provides deeper insight into sustainability 
impacts as both risks and opportunities.
Prioritisation of material issues is guided by a structured 
scoring methodology that combines stakeholder feedback 
with risk assessment. For each topic, we consider:
	
Scale
Severity of the impact.
	
Scope
Extent of affected people, assets or geographies.
	
Irremediable Character
Difficulty of reversing or mitigating harm, especially for 
negative impacts.
	
Likelihood
Probability of occurrence.
These criteria are applied across impacts, risks and 
opportunities, and then integrated with our ERM framework 
to align topic scoring with risk registers, emerging risk 
monitoring and capital allocation decisions. This ensures that 
ESG topics with high risk or opportunity implications receive 
appropriate governance and management attention.

Risk Management Process
Risk events are systematically identified, assessed and 
prioritised based on their likelihood of occurrence and 
potential impact on established objectives. Following 
the identification of risks, a thorough description is 
provided and identified risks are assessed based on the 
Risk Evaluation Framework to estimate their potential 
impact and likelihood of occurrence. Specific control 
measures are evaluated to mitigate each of the risks. 
The combination of the potential impact of a risk and its 
likelihood is used to determine its intensity and scores 
are calculated to carry out analysis. We conduct a 
comprehensive analysis semi-annually, supplemented 
by selective reviews every quarter, ensuring a robust 
and adaptive assessment process. Using this process 
and in alignment with SEBI LODR, IRB’s ERM framework 
addresses risks under 5 categories of risks.

India’s transition from WPI to Producer Price Index (PPI)
Context
The IRB’s annual horizon scanning exercise identified 
distinct developments in India’s price index framework 
that create unprecedented uncertainty for infrastructure 
concessions whose revenue streams are indexed to 
wholesale price benchmarks. This exercise is supported by 
analysis of regulatory publications from NHAI, the Ministry 
of Commerce and Industry (DPIIT), and MoSPI. These 
developments were reviewed by the IRB’s Finance and 
Risk functions in and formally elevated to the emerging risk 
register on the basis that they represent a structural change 
to the indexation architecture of infrastructure concession 
agreements – a change arising from a reconciliation of 
the linking factor with data published by the Office of the 
Economic Adviser and couldn’t have been anticipated when 
the older concession agreements were finalised.
Price index linkage and the risk of indexation 
underperformance relative to actual cost inflation have 
long been features of India’s infrastructure concession 
landscape. What elevates the current situation to 
an emerging risk of a different and unprecedented 
character is due to recent and specific development as 
mentioned below.
Recently, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry released 
India’s inaugural Producer Price Index data, marking 
the commencement of a formally announced transition 
from WPI – the benchmark embedded in all major NHAI 
concession agreements for annual toll rate revision – to 
PPI over a five-year horizon. The WPI will be progressively 
discontinued by 2031. The PPI, while methodologically 
superior in its measurement of producer-level price 
dynamics and aligned with international standards including 
IMF recommendations, differs structurally from WPI in its 
basket composition, stage-of-production measurement, 
and treatment of services. The trajectory of PPI relative to 
WPI across commodity cycles is not yet established given 
the absence of a PPI historical time series under the new 
2022-23 base. The Company notes that existing concession 
agreements reference WPI specifically, and the contractual 
and regulatory pathway for rebasing toll indexation to 
PPI is ultimately a policy question for NHAI and MoRTH. 
This introduces an unprecedented period of indexation 
uncertainty that the Company is actively monitoring. 
Mitigation
	
Constructive regulatory engagement 
The Company actively participates in industry 
forums, including representations through relevant 
associations and direct engagement with NHAI 
and MoRTH, to contribute to the development 
of practical and equitable frameworks for the 
WPI-to-PPI transition in concession agreement 
contexts. The Company believes that the 
government’s commitment to a consultative 
approach to major policy transitions provides an 
appropriate pathway for industry concerns to be 
addressed constructively.
	
Concession agreement gap analysis 
The Company notes that it approaches this matter 
as a constructive stakeholder in India’s infrastructure 
development ecosystem and is confident that the 
government and NHAI, through their established 
frameworks for concessionaire engagement, will 
develop an equitable and operationally practical 
resolution to the indexation transition. A review 
of all active concession and project agreements 
informs the Company’s legal preparedness without 
prejudging any outcome. 
Potential Business Impact
	
Indexation rebasing creates uncertainty on toll 
rates: For the Company’s BOT and HAM concession 
assets whose toll revision formula references WPI, 
the transition to PPI creates a period uncertainty 
during which the annual escalation is applicable to 
toll rates.
	
Concession agreement gap: The model concession 
agreements doesn’t contain provisions specifically 
governing the scenario of the referenced WPI series 
being discontinued and replaced by an alternative 
index. This creates a contractual gap that will need 
to be addressed – through regulatory guidance, 
concession agreement amendments, circular or any 
other suitable mechanism.

Strategy
IRB has defined its short-term (0–5 years), medium-term 
(5–10 years), and long-term (Beyond 10 years) strategy 
after a comprehensive peer benchmarking exercise. These 
time frames form the basis for assessing the materiality of 
climate-related risks and opportunities and are embedded 
into risk reviews, strategic planning, and investment 
decision frameworks.
Based on the IPCC RCP Scenarios and seven NGFS climate 
scenarios, IRB has proactively identified a spectrum of

Financial Disclosures (TCFD).
For identifying and assessing physical risks, IRB has 
considered IPCC’s Representative Concentration Pathways 
(RCP), RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5. For transition risks, IRB utilised 
India’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), Below 
2°C Scenario, NGFS Current Policy and Net Zero 2050 
Scenarios. We mapped the plausible business impact of the 
following categories of risks and opportunities:
Physical Risks
Physical risks are a result of short-term catastrophes (acute) 
or long-term variations in climate patterns (chronic). Acute 
physical risks are those that are triggered by a specific event, 
such as extreme weather events like cyclones, storms or 
floods. Whereas longer-term changes in climatic patterns 
(e.g. prolonged higher temperatures) may produce sea level 
rise or chronic heat waves, which are referred to as chronic 
physical hazards.
Transition Risks
Transition risks are enterprise risks that arise as a result of 
societal and economic transformations toward a low carbon, 
more environmentally friendly future. These risks can include 
policy and regulatory and legal risks, technological risks, 
market risks and reputational risks. These areas can vary 
in terms of their type, focus and geographical acceptance, 
which can have a financial implication on our business.

assessments and continuous monitoring activities designed

mitigation measures.

structured lines-of-defence model, under which business

management processes.

from technology providers, service partners, consultants 
and other third parties with access to systems or 
information assets.
Information security considerations are incorporated 
into vendor onboarding, procurement and technology 
engagement processes through risk-based due diligence 
and control assessments. These evaluations support the 
identification and management of potential cybersecurity 
risks arising from external relationships and contribute to 
strengthening supply chain resilience.
The Company continues to enhance third-party 
cybersecurity oversight in recognition of the increasing 
interconnectedness of digital ecosystems and 
infrastructure operations.
Cyber Risk Management
Cybersecurity risks are actively managed through a 
combination of preventive, detective and responsive 
controls. The Company undertakes periodic Vulnerability 
Assessment and Penetration Testing (VAPT), security 
monitoring activities, control reviews and risk assessments 
to identify vulnerabilities and strengthen cyber resilience 
across its technology landscape.
Security measures are continuously enhanced to address 
emerging risks affecting digital infrastructure, enterprise 
applications, cloud environments and operational systems. 
Cybersecurity considerations are integrated into broader risk 
management processes to support proactive identification, 
mitigation and monitoring of cyber threats that may impact 
business continuity and operational performance.
Cyber Awareness & Human Firewall
Recognising that employees are a critical line of defence 
against cyber threats, IRB continues to strengthen its human 
firewall through structured awareness and capability-
building initiatives.
Regular cybersecurity awareness programmes, policy 
communications and training interventions help employees 
understand emerging threats, cybersecurity responsibilities 
and secure digital practices. These initiatives support 
the development of a strong cybersecurity culture 
while reducing human-related security risks such as 
phishing, social engineering and unauthorised disclosure 
of information.
Through continuous engagement and awareness efforts, 
the Company seeks to embed responsible digital behaviour 
across all levels of the organisation.
Cyber Incident Management
IRB has established structured processes for managing 
cybersecurity incidents and responding to emerging 
threats. These processes define responsibilities and 
protocols for incident identification, classification, 
escalation, investigation, reporting and recovery.
The Company's incident management framework follows a 
systematic lifecycle approach encompassing preparedness, 
detection, response, investigation, reporting and recovery. 
Insights derived from incident reviews, assessments and 
monitoring activities are used to strengthen controls, 
improve response-readiness and support continuous 
enhancement of cybersecurity capabilities.
Business Continuity and Cyber Resilience
Maintaining operational continuity across toll operations, 
project execution activities and corporate functions is a 
key priority for IRB. Business Continuity Planning (BCP) and 
Disaster Recovery (DR) mechanisms have been established 
to support resilience against cyber incidents, technology 
disruptions and other operational events.
These arrangements include backup protocols, recovery 
procedures, incident response strategies and resilience 
testing activities designed to minimise operational 
disruption and facilitate timely restoration of critical systems 
and services. Periodic testing and review of continuity 
arrangements help ensure preparedness and strengthen 
organisational resilience.
Information Security Audit and Assurance
The effectiveness of IRB's Information Security 
Management System is periodically evaluated through 
internal audits, management reviews, surveillance 
assessments and independent external evaluations. 
These assessments examine governance processes, 
risk management practices, technical controls, 
access management mechanisms and information 
protection measures.
Findings from audit and assurance activities are used to 
strengthen controls, implement corrective actions and 
drive continual improvement of the information security 
framework. This process supports ongoing alignment with 
ISO 27001 requirements, evolving regulatory expectations 
and emerging industry best practices.

We have instituted a structured ESG governance framework 
anchored in Board-level oversight and supported by

other relevant Board committees, in line with applicable 
regulatory expectations.

ESG priorities, recommends key policies and targets to 
the Board, and reviews performance against material 
ESG indicators and regulatory disclosures, including the 
Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report (BRSR).

have established an ESG Committee comprising senior 
executives responsible for driving the sustainability agenda

Monitoring and Evaluation, Health & Safety, Environment, 
Operations and Risk Management.

least quarterly, and more frequently when required. 
Its deliberations and key decisions are reported to the 
Managing Director and, through him, to the Board or 
relevant Board committees.

We leverage a networked governance model with cross-functional participation to ensure that ESG responsibilities are 
entrenched in business operations. Under the ESG Committee, functional heads and business unit leaders act as ESG 
representatives within their respective domains, supported by designated ESG single points of contact (SPOCs).

We embed internationally recognised management systems 
across  all our project sites, toll plazas and operational

Maximising Asset Availability
We closely monitor asset performance to maintain seamless 
toll operations and high network availability. We capture 
real-time data and leverage automated reconciliation 
to improve the accuracy, efficiency and transparency 
of toll transactions.  
Digitally-enabled Toll Operations
We have strengthened toll operations through FASTag, 
RFID-enabled systems and advanced toll management 
platforms across our plazas. FASTag penetration exceeds 
97%, enabling faster, contactless transactions while 
reducing congestion, vehicle idling, emissions, cash 
handling and manual intervention.
Integrated digital platforms support real-time traffic 
and revenue monitoring, accurate and tamper-resistant 
collections, faster lane clearance and improved toll 
throughput. These capabilities enhance financial control, 
asset utilisation and commuter experience while advancing 
our alignment with national infrastructure priorities, 
including Gati Shakti, Bharatmala and the National 
Logistics Policy.

Infrastructure Beyond Roads
Sindhudurg Airport
Marking our entry into multimodal infrastructure, we 
developed Sindhudurg Airport near the Goa-Maharashtra 
border through IRB Sindhudurg Airport Private Limited. 
The airport is fully operational for scheduled and non-
scheduled commercial flights and provides comprehensive 
infrastructure support for domestic and chartered services.
Designed as a 24×7, all-weather IFR facility, the airport 
supports day-and-night operations and has published RNP 
approach procedures. Its six parking bays can accommodate 
Code C aircraft, including the B737 MAX and A320 family, 
with provision for night parking.
Strategically located, Sindhudurg Airport serves as an 
efficient and cost-effective gateway to the Konkan region, 
including Goa. It also supports our long-term strategy to 
expand multimodal logistics capabilities, with potential future 
integration across freight corridors and road, rail and air 
transport networks.

Recognising Performance Holistically
We follow a blended performance appraisal methodology 
that combines structured assessment with managerial 
judgement. Instead of applying a uniform forced-
distribution or bell-curve approach, managers evaluate 
performance in the context of roles, responsibilities and 
individual contributions.
The assessment considers business outcomes alongside 
tenure, sustained effort, consistency, initiative, work ethic, 
attitude and alignment with our values. It also recognises 
employees who take ownership, go beyond defined 
responsibilities and strengthen our organisational culture.
This approach enables fairer and more credible 
evaluations while ensuring deserving employees receive 
appropriate recognition. It supports employee motivation, 
strengthens engagement and reinforces our Employee 
Value Proposition by acknowledging the full scope of each 
person’s contribution.
Supporting Employee Well-being
During FY 2025-26, we invested prudently in employee 
wellness programmes to support the physical, mental and 
emotional well-being of our people. We plan to expand 
these efforts through new initiatives and enhanced benefits 
that help employees thrive personally and professionally.
A Workplace Built on Respect
We are committed to maintaining a safe, inclusive and 
respectful workplace founded on fairness, dignity and 
ethical conduct. As an equal opportunity employer, we 
prohibit abuse, harassment and discrimination based 
on race, religion, caste, gender identity or expression, 
sexual orientation, genetics, age or any other legally 
protected characteristic. 
We regularly review the composition of our workforce to 
promote diversity and inclusion. This enables us to create 
an environment where employees feel valued, secure and 
empowered to contribute to our success.
Safeguarding Human Rights
Our Human Rights Policy protects the fundamental rights 
of employees, consumers, communities and value chain 
partners. It is aligned with the United Nations Guiding 
Principles on Business and Human Rights and reflects 
our commitment to respecting, supporting and promoting 
human rights across our operations.
We extend these expectations to suppliers and business 
partners through our responsible sourcing practices. 
Suppliers are expected to treat their employees with 
dignity, respect and fairness, helping embed ethical 
conduct and inclusivity across our value chain.
Preventing Workplace Harassment
Our Prevention of Sexual Harassment Policy reinforces 
our commitment to a harassment-free workplace. An 
Internal Committee, led by the Presiding Officer, addresses 
grievances fairly and promptly. We take appropriate 
action against violations to uphold employee safety, trust 
and dignity.
Supporting Expectant Mothers
The Company recognises the valuable contribution of 
women employees in its growth and is committed to 
supporting them during their transition to motherhood. 
To enable expectant mothers to care for their new-born 
babies while maintaining career continuity, maternity 
leave is provided for 12 weeks prior to childbirth and 
12 weeks following childbirth.  This benefit is a testament 
to Company’s  commitment  to employee and family well-
being and supports a healthy balance between parental 
responsibilities and professional commitments. 
Aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 8, our 
maternity leave policy promotes decent work, employee 
well-being and inclusive economic growth.
Investing in our People for a Sustainable Future
Our people are central to our performance and long-term 
progress. By supporting their development, safety and well-
being, we strengthen our organisation while contributing to 
a more resilient construction and engineering sector.
As we grow, we remain focused on building an inclusive, 
secure and empowering workplace where employees can 
realise their potential. This approach enables us to combine 
responsible growth with sustainable practices that create 
lasting value for our people, stakeholders and communities.
Safety Leadership and Governance
Safety is a core organisational value that supports 
operational excellence, workforce well-being and 
sustainable value creation. Across our offices, project sites, 
toll plazas and operational assets, our Zero Harm Vision 
guides our commitment to incident-free operations. We 
believe every employee, contractor and stakeholder has the 
right to a safe and healthy workplace and to return home 
safely each day.
We integrate safety performance into our operational 
review framework through defined indicators and targets. 
Our Environment, Health and Safety (EHS) framework 
supports an incident-free, environmentally responsible 
and socially accountable operating environment across 
the infrastructure lifecycle. Our safety management 
systems comply with applicable statutory requirements 
and sector-specific guidance, including the NHAI Safety 
Manual, MoRTH requirements, relevant IRC guidelines and 
recognised industry practices.
Our Health, Safety and Welfare Policy forms the foundation 
of our Occupational Health and Safety framework. It 
is supported by procedures, guidelines, manuals and 
operational controls. Employees, contractors and site 
representatives share responsibility for identifying 
risks, promoting safe behaviour and strengthening 
workplace safety.
Dedicated EHS teams operate across business units and 
project locations. They work with project leadership to 
implement interventions suited to the risks associated 
with each project and location. Safety performance is 
reviewed monthly through management forums, keeping 
occupational health and safety integrated with strategic 
decision-making and enterprise risk management.
Periodic management reviews, project oversight 
mechanisms and EHS Committees strengthen leadership 
accountability. Project-level Safety Committees include 
representatives from management, project teams and 
subcontractors. They review performance, encourage 
workforce participation and oversee corrective and 
continuous improvement measures.
Contractor safety is managed through contractual 
requirements, training, inspections and audits. These 
mechanisms help maintain consistent safety standards 
across our workforce and value chain.

Building a Proactive Safety Culture
We believe sustainable safety performance depends on making safety part of everyday decision-making. We are therefore 
progressing from compliance-led practices towards a proactive, risk-based and behaviour-focused approach that engages 
employees, contractors and leadership teams.
Drawing on leading practices across the global construction and engineering sector, our safety culture is built around three 
interconnected pillars.
Engage
We encourage active participation 
through Safety Committees, 
toolbox talks, site inspections, 
workforce consultations, contractor 
engagement and monthly EHS 
communications. Employees and 
workers are encouraged to identify

contribute to improvement initiatives.
Educate
Continuous learning is integral 
to our safety culture. Employees, 
contractors and visitors receive 
structured EHS inductions,

job learning.
Empower
We encourage employees and 
contractors to report hazards, 
near misses and unsafe 
conditions without hesitation. 
Structured reporting mechanisms, 
incident investigations and 
leadership engagement enable 
them to contribute actively  
to safer workplaces.
Our proactive safety culture is centred on six strategic 
outcomes:
	
Risk prevention through the systematic identification and 
mitigation of hazards before incidents occur
	
Workforce well-being through safe, healthy and 
supportive workplaces that promote physical, mental and 
emotional well-being
	
Regulatory compliance through adherence to legal 
requirements, client specifications, industry guidelines 
and recognised management system standards
	
Operational excellence through stronger execution, 
operating discipline and business continuity
	
Stakeholder trust through responsible conduct 
and greater confidence among employees, clients, 
regulators, investors and communities
	
Cultural transformation through participation, 
continuous learning and personal ownership of 
safety responsibilities
Employees and workers are expected to raise concerns 
immediately when they observe unsafe conditions, unsafe 
acts or situations involving imminent risk. Work may be 
paused and escalated through the appropriate supervisory 
and EHS channels until the hazard is assessed and suitable 
controls are implemented.
By enabling employees and contractors to speak up, 
intervene and participate in risk mitigation, we reinforce 
personal accountability and embed safety within 
operational decision-making across all project locations.
Integrated Safety and Risk Controls
Our EHS framework brings together risk management, 
workforce participation, regulatory compliance and 
operational discipline to prevent incidents and strengthen 
safety performance.
We conduct internal and external audits, including 
Integrated Management System audits and client 
assessments, in line with ISO 45001 requirements. Project-
specific Safety Management Plans and Traffic Management 
Plans address operational risks and client expectations. 
Together, these measures reinforce accountability, 
improve workforce engagement and support a resilient 
safety culture.
Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA)
Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment is central 
to our safety approach. It enables us to systematically 
identify, evaluate and control workplace hazards across 
project locations.
The process covers routine and non-routine activities and 
involves design engineers, construction teams, planners, 
EHS professionals and contract workers. This collaborative 
approach keeps assessments practical, site-specific and 
responsive to changing operating conditions.
Risks are assessed before work begins and reviewed 
throughout project execution. This supports informed 
decisions on safety procedures, operational controls, 
resource allocation and workforce protection, while 
helping us respond to emerging risks and strengthen 
operational resilience.

Strengthening Safety on the Ground
EHS Induction Room 
We have established dedicated EHS induction rooms at each construction site to familiarise employees and workers with 
safety systems, operating guidelines, emergency procedures, incident reporting and applicable regulatory requirements. 
The sessions clarify individual responsibilities and reinforce the importance of reporting incidents and near misses.
By creating a structured learning environment before work begins, we strengthen workforce preparedness and embed 
safety awareness into daily operations.
Scaling Best Practices Across Projects
We systematically identify and replicate effective EHS interventions across project locations. During FY 2025-26, several 
proven measures were extended across sites to strengthen safety performance and operational discipline.
At operational facilities, barricades were installed around hot mix plant areas to restrict unauthorised access, improve hazard 
communication and strengthen site controls. 
Monthly EHS Alerts are shared across project locations 
to communicate incident learnings, preventive measures 
and key safety messages. These alerts are also issued in 
Hindi to improve accessibility and understanding across the 
workforce. This strengthens engagement, organisational 
learning and a proactive safety culture.

To eliminate the serious risks of fire, explosion, and burn 
injuries during maintenance activities and while working near 
bitumen tanks at Hot Mix Plants, this safety alert is issued to 
reinforce safe operating procedures, permit compliance, and 
awareness among employees and workers.
Hazards & Risks Involved: 
❖Overheating of bitumen leading to fire 
❖Boil-over / splashing of hot bitumen causing severe burns
❖Pressure build-up inside tank due to blocked vents or 
heating
❖Release of toxic gases (fumes during heating or maintenance)
❖Oxygen deficiency inside tank during confined space entry
❖Static electricity accumulation leading to spark ignition
❖Leakage from valves, pipelines, or tank joints
❖Failure of temperature control systems
❖Burner malfunction or fuel leakage
❖Backfire from burner system
❖Contact with hot surfaces (tank body, pipelines, valves)
❖Manual handling injuries during maintenance work
❖Poor visibility due to fumes or smoke
❖Inadequate lighting in work area
❖Noise hazard from plant machinery
❖Trip hazards due to hoses, cables, and uneven surfaces
❖Environmental pollution due to bitumen spill or fire
❖Improper storage of fuel near tank area
❖Lack of emergency access/egress routes
❖Inadequate training or awareness among workers
❖Failure of firefighting systems or unavailability of equipment
❖Heat stress for workers working near hot surfaces
❖Fatigue leading to unsafe acts
❖Delayed detection of fire due to lack of monitoring

✓Stop work immediately if unsafe condition is observed

✓Ensure earthing/grounding of tank and equipment to prevent

❑Do not enter confined space alone or without attendant
❑Do not operate equipment if leakage of bitumen or fuel is 
observed

activities

Safety by Design
#Case Study 1: 
Preventing Risk at the Source
The Context
Hot mix plants involve high-temperature processes, 
moving equipment and multiple operational hazards. 
Uncontrolled access to these areas can expose 
personnel to serious injury, interfere with equipment 
movement and disrupt operations.
Our Intervention
We implemented a structured barricading system 
around the hot mix plant area to strengthen 
access control and create a safer operating 
environment. The initiative was designed as 
an engineering control under the Hierarchy of 
Controls, addressing risk at source rather than 
relying primarily on individual behaviour or personal 
protective equipment.
Key Measures
	
Robust physical barricades around the 
operational area
	
Restricted entry for authorised and 
trained personnel
	
Prominent warning signage communicating 
hazards and safe practices
	
Clear segregation of personnel movement from 
plant operations
	
Defined access points to improve supervision and 
site control
Safety Outcomes
The initiative strengthened access control 
around a critical operational area and reduced 
personnel exposure to moving equipment and 
plant-related hazards. It also improved hazard 
communication, reinforced compliance with site 
safety procedures and supported greater awareness 
of restricted zones.
By separating workforce movement from operational 
activities, the barricading system improved discipline 
around the plant and reduced the potential for 
unauthorised entry and operational interference.
Key Takeaway
Physical barricading provides a preventive 
layer of protection by isolating people from 
hazards at source. This initiative reflects our 
focus on proactive risk management and 
demonstrates how practical engineering 
controls can strengthen safety performance 
across project sites.

#Case Study 3: 
Enabling Safer and More Disciplined Vehicle 
Movement
The Context
The movement and parking of Heavy Motor Vehicles 
within plant premises can create congestion, restrict 
access and increase the risk of vehicle-related 
incidents. Unorganised parking may also lead to 
unsafe interaction between vehicles, equipment 
and pedestrians.
Our Intervention
We developed a dedicated parking zone for Heavy 
Motor Vehicles within the plant premises. The area 
incorporates a structured parking layout, designated 
movement routes, signage and ground markings to 
improve traffic management and maintain orderly 
vehicle movement.
The initiative combines engineering and 
administrative controls by creating a 
segregated parking area and establishing clear 
operating practices.
Safety Outcomes
The Initiative:
	
Improved traffic management within the plant 
	
Reduced the risk of vehicle-related incidents 
	
Enabled systematic vehicle movement 
and parking 
	
Reduced congestion and improved access 
	
Strengthened discipline through signage 
and markings  
Key Takeaway
Dedicated parking and controlled vehicle 
movement reduce interaction between 
vehicles, equipment and pedestrians, 
supporting safer and more efficient 
plant operations.
Monitoring and Continuous Improvement
Strengthening Assurance and Compliance
Continuous monitoring and independent verification 
strengthen the effectiveness of our safety management 
systems. We follow a standardised Integrated Management 
System procedure for reporting, investigating and 
analysing incidents and near misses, enabling root-cause 
identification and timely corrective action.
We increasingly use technology to share safety alerts, good 
practices and training content. During FY 2025-26, we also 
commenced implementation of a compliance monitoring 
tool to track applicable regulatory requirements and 
strengthen oversight across operations.
Internal audits were conducted across all project locations 
during the final quarter to assess compliance with IMS 
requirements, EHS standards and statutory obligations. 
External ISO audits were completed as scheduled, 
with zero major or minor non-conformities, reflecting 
strong operational discipline and the maturity of our 
management systems.
Learning from Near Misses
Near-miss reporting is a key leading indicator of safety 
performance. Each reported event helps us identify 
underlying hazards, strengthen controls and prevent injuries 
or operational disruption.
All near misses are investigated through root-cause 
analysis, followed by corrective action and communication 
of lessons across project locations. This reinforces risk 
awareness and supports a predictive, prevention-focused 
safety culture.
Protecting Occupational Health
Our employees and contractors operate across 
construction sites, toll plazas, plants and project locations, 
where they may be exposed to heat stress, dust, noise, 
vibration, ergonomic strain, fatigue, traffic-related risks and 
other site-specific hazards.
We manage these risks through engineering and 
administrative controls, workplace monitoring, personal 
protective equipment, health surveillance and workforce 
awareness. Occupational health risks are periodically 
assessed through HIRA and incorporated into operational 
planning and control measures.
Prepared for Emergencies
We maintain emergency preparedness and response 
procedures covering evacuation, safety protocols and 
medical support for different emergency scenarios. 
Routine mock drills, response exercises and training 
help employees and contractors respond effectively and 
minimise operational disruption.
These measures strengthen our preparedness, 
response capability and operational resilience across 
project locations.
These interventions demonstrate IRB's commitment to translating lessons learned into practical improvements that reduce 
risk exposure and strengthen workplace safety.

Identifying Significant Suppliers
During FY 2025-26, we established a structured 
methodology to identify significant suppliers for 
sustainability assessment and monitoring. In line with the 
SEBI Value Chain Disclosure Framework and Industry 
Standards Forum guidance, suppliers individually 
accounting for 2% or more of procurement expenditure 
were classified as significant.
This process identified 11 significant suppliers, together 
representing approximately 51% of total procurement 
expenditure. The assessment covered publicly available 
information on environmental management, climate 
commitments, occupational health and safety, human rights, 
labour practices, business ethics and governance.
The exercise established a baseline for future engagement 
and enables us to focus on suppliers with the greatest 
business relevance and potential value chain impact.
The assessment focused on publicly available disclosures 
and information relating to environmental management, 
climate commitments, occupational health and safety, 
human rights, labour practices, business ethics and 
governance systems. The exercise established a baseline 
for future supplier engagement and enhanced visibility of 
sustainability-related risks and opportunities across the 
value chain.
The desktop assessment revealed differing levels of ESG 
disclosure maturity across supplier categories. Suppliers 
operating in regulated sectors such as energy, cement and 
steel generally maintain publicly available sustainability 
disclosures and established ESG management systems. 
In contrast, privately held construction, infrastructure and 
industrial suppliers often exhibit more limited public ESG 
reporting, creating opportunities for future engagement, 
awareness and capability building.
The assessment highlighted differing levels of ESG 
disclosure maturity across supplier categories.
Supplier Assessment Insights
The assessment indicated varying levels of ESG disclosure 
maturity across supplier categories. Suppliers in highly 
regulated sectors, including fuel, energy and cement, 
generally maintained established sustainability governance 
systems, public disclosures and climate commitments.
Construction and infrastructure service providers had 
comparatively limited public ESG disclosures. This may 
reflect lower levels of formal reporting among privately held 
businesses rather than weaker sustainability performance.
Steel suppliers represented approximately 11% of 
procurement expenditure. Of this, around 8% was 
associated with privately held suppliers using a combination 
of Electric Arc Furnace and integrated Direct Reduced Iron 
production routes. These pathways have different energy 
and emissions profiles and provide useful insights into the 
environmental characteristics of key construction materials.
A significant share of assessed procurement expenditure 
was also linked to suppliers with investment-grade financial 
profiles, supporting supply chain resilience and business 
continuity. The assessment did not identify any significant 
supplier requiring a formal corrective action plan or 
termination of the relationship.
