3.10	 Provisions
	
Provisions are recognised when the Company has a 
present obligation (legal or constructive) as a result of 
a past event, it is probable that an outflow of resources 
embodying economic benefits will be required to settle 
the obligation and a reliable estimate can be made of 
the amount of the obligation. The expense relating to a 
provision is presented in the statement of profit and loss 
net of any reimbursement.
	
If the effect of the time value of money is material, 
provisions are discounted using a current pre-tax rate 
that reflects, when appropriate, the risks specific to 
the liability. When discounting is used, the increase in 
the provision due to the passage of time is recognised 
as a finance cost. Provisions are reviewed at each 
balance sheet date and adjusted to reflect the current 
best estimates.
3.11	 Investments in subsidiaries and joint ventures
	
The Company accounts for the investments in equity 
shares of subsidiaries and joint ventures at cost 
in accordance with Ind AS 27- Separate Financial 
Statements. The Company reviews its carrying value of 
investments carried at amortised cost annually, or more 
frequently when there is indication for impairment. If the 
recoverable amount is less than its carrying amount, 
the impairment loss is accounted for. On disposal 
of investments in subsidiaries and joint venture, the 
difference between net disposal proceeds and the 
carrying amounts are recognised in the Standalone 
Statement of Profit and Loss.
	
From the quarter ended December 31, 2024, pursuant 
to the requirements of Ind AS 28, “Investment in Joint 
ventures and Associates” read with Ind AS 27 “Separate 
Financial Statements”, the Company’s assessed its 
eligible joint venture investments are measured at fair 
value through profit and loss in accordance with Ind 
AS 109 rather than using cost method (Refer note 29). 
As per Ind AS 28, this election is used for investments 
wherein there is demonstrable features such as, fair 
value being the primary measurement attribute used, 
fair value information of the eligible investments being 
used internally used by the Company’s key management 
personnel and also being provided to the investors. In 
addition, the Company also considers presence of certain 
typical characteristics, including, having more than one 
investment, to diversify the risk portfolio and maximise 
returns; having multiple non-related party investors 
whose object is to maximise investment opportunities; 
and having ownership interests in the form of equity or 
similar interests.
3.12	 Retirement and other employee benefits
	
Employee benefits include salaries, wages, contribution 
to provident fund, gratuity, leave encashment towards 
un-availed leave, compensated absences, post-
retirement medical benefits and other terminal benefits.
	
Short-term employee benefits
	
Wages and salaries, including non-monetary benefits 
that are expected to be settled within 12 months after 
the end of the period in which the employees render the 
related service are recognised in respect of employees’ 
services up to the end of the reporting period and are 
measured at the amounts expected to be paid when 
the liabilities are settled. The liabilities are presented 
as current employee benefit obligations in the balance 
sheet. Liabilities recognised in respect of short-term 
employee benefits are measured at the undiscounted 
amount of the benefits expected to be paid in exchange 
for the related service.
	
i.	
Defined contribution plan
	
	
Retirement benefits in the form of provident 
fund are a defined contribution scheme and the 
contributions are charged to the standalone 
statement of profit and loss of the period when 
the employee renders related services. There are 
no other obligations other than the contribution 
payable to the respective authorities.
	
Deferred tax
	
Deferred tax is recognised in respect of temporary 
differences between the tax bases of assets and 
liabilities and their carrying amounts for financial 
reporting purposes at the reporting date.
	
Deferred tax liabilities are recognised for all taxable 
temporary differences, except:
•	 When the deferred tax liability arises from the initial 
recognition of goodwill or an asset or liability in a 
transaction that is not a business combination and 
at the time of the transaction, affects neither the 
accounting profit nor taxable profit or loss.
•	 In respect of taxable temporary differences associated 
with investments in subsidiaries and joint-ventures, 
when the timing of the reversal of the temporary 
differences can be controlled and it is probable that 
the temporary differences will not reverse in the 
foreseeable future.
	
Deferred tax assets are recognised for all deductible 
temporary differences, the carry forward of unused 
tax credits and any unused tax losses. The Company 
recognises a deferred tax asset only to the extent that it 
has sufficient taxable temporary differences or there is 
convincing other evidence that sufficient taxable profit 
will be available against which such deferred tax asset 
can be realised, except
•	 When the deferred tax asset relating to the 
deductible temporary difference arises from the initial 
recognition of an asset or liability in a transaction that 
is not a business combination and, at the time of the 
transaction affects neither the accounting profit nor 
taxable profit or loss and does not give rise to equal 
taxable and deductible temporary differences.
	
The carrying amount of deferred tax assets is reviewed 
at each reporting date and reduced to the extent that it 
is no longer probable that sufficient taxable profit will 
be available to allow all or part of the deferred tax asset 
to be utilised. Unrecognised deferred tax assets are re-
assessed at each reporting date and are recognised to 
the extent that it has become probable that future taxable 
profits will allow the deferred tax asset to be recovered. 
In assessing the recoverability of deferred tax assets, 
the company relies on the same forecast assumptions 
used elsewhere in the financial statements and in other 
management reports, which, among other things, reflect 
the potential impact of climate-related development on 
the business, such as increased cost of production as a 
result of measures to reduce carbon emission.
	
Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured at the 
tax rates that are expected to apply in the year when 
the asset is realised or the liability is settled, based 
on tax rates (and tax laws) that have been enacted or 
substantively enacted at the reporting date.
	
Deferred tax relating to items recognised outside profit 
or loss is recognised outside profit or loss (either in 
other comprehensive income or in equity). Deferred tax 
items are recognised in correlation to the underlying 
transaction either in OCI or directly in equity.
	
Deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities are offset 
if a legally enforceable right exists to set off current tax 
assets against current tax liabilities and the deferred 
taxes relate to the same taxable entity and the same 
taxation authority.
	
On March 30, 2019, MCA has issued amendment 
regarding the income tax Uncertainty over Income Tax 
Treatments. The notification clarifies the recognition and 
measurement requirements when there is uncertainty 
over income tax treatments. In assessing the uncertainty, 
an entity shall consider whether it is probable that a 
taxation authority will accept the uncertain tax treatment. 
This notification is effective for annual reporting 
periods beginning on or after April 1, 2019. As per the 
Company’s assessment, there are no material income 
tax uncertainties over income tax treatments.

Debt instrument at FVTOCI
	
A ‘debt instrument’ is classified at FVTOCI if both of the 
following criteria are met:
	
a)	
The objective of the business model is achieved

b)

recognition and is irrevocable.
	
If the Company decides to classify an equity instrument

standalone statement of profit and loss, even on sale

cumulative gain or loss within equity.
	
Equity instruments included within the FVTPL category 
are measured at fair value with all changes recognised

used to measure the defined benefit

Subsequent measurement
	
The measurement of financial liabilities depends on their 
classification, as described below:
	
Financial liabilities at fair value through profit or loss
	
Financial liabilities at fair value through profit or loss 
include financial liabilities held for trading and financial 
liabilities designated upon initial recognition as at fair 
value through profit or loss. Financial liabilities are 
classified as held for trading if they are incurred for the 
purpose of repurchasing in the near term.
	
Loans and borrowings
	
This is the category most relevant to the Company. After 
initial recognition, interest-bearing loans and borrowings 
are subsequently measured at amortised cost using the 
EIR method. Gains and losses are recognised in profit 
or loss when the liabilities are derecognised as well as 
through the EIR amortisation process. Amortised cost 
is calculated by taking into account any discount or 
premium on acquisition and fees or costs that are an 
integral part of the EIR. The EIR amortisation is included 
as finance costs in the statement of profit and loss.
	
This category generally applies to borrowings. For more 
information refer Note 15.
	
Derecognition
	
A financial liability is derecognised when the obligation 
under the liability is discharged or cancelled or expires. 
When an existing financial liability is replaced by another 
from the same lender on substantially different terms, 
or the terms of an existing liability are substantially 
modified, such an exchange or modification is treated 
as the derecognition of the original liability and the 
recognition of a new liability. The difference in the 
respective carrying amounts is recognised in the 
standalone statement of profit and loss.
	
Offsetting of financial instruments
	
Financial assets and financial liabilities are offset and 
the net amount is reported in the balance sheet if 
there is a currently enforceable legal right to offset 
the recognised amounts and there is an intention to 
settle on a net basis, to realise the assets and settle the 
liabilities simultaneously.
3.14	 Contingent consideration receivable
	
Contingent consideration is classified as an asset 
and is measured at fair value on the transaction date. 
Subsequently, contingent consideration is remeasured 
to fair value at each reporting date, with changes 
included in the statement of profit and loss.
3.15	 Cash and cash equivalents
	
Cash and cash equivalent in the balance sheet comprise 
cash at banks and on hand and short-term deposits with 
an original maturity of three months or less, which are 
subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value.
	
For the purpose of the statement of cash flows, cash 
and cash equivalents consist of cash and short-term 
deposits, as defined above as they are considered an 
integral part of the Company’s cash management.
3.16	 Assets held for sale:
	
Non-current assets or disposal groups comprising of 
assets and liabilities are classified as ‘held for sale’ 
when all of the following criteria’s are met: (i) decision 
has been made to sell. (ii) the assets are available for 
immediate sale in its present condition. (iii) The asset 
or disposal company is being marketed at a reasonable 
price in relation to its fair value (iv) sale has been agreed 
or is expected to be concluded within 12 months of the 
Balance Sheet date and (v) It is unlikely that significant 
changes to the plan will be made or that the plan will 
be withdrawn. These are measured at the lower of their 
carrying amount and fair value less costs to sale. Costs 
to sell are the incremental costs directly attributable to 
the disposal of assets (disposal group), excluding finance 
cost and income tax expenses.
3.17	 Earnings per share
	
Basic earnings per share are calculated by dividing the 
net profit or loss for the period attributable to equity 
shareholders by the weighted average number of equity 
shares outstanding during the period.
	
For the purpose of calculating diluted earnings per 
share, the net profit or loss for the period attributable to 
equity shareholders and the weighted average number 
of shares outstanding during the period are adjusted for 
the effects of all dilutive potential equity shares.
	
The weighted average number of equity shares 
outstanding during the year is adjusted for events such 
as bonus issue, bonus element in a rights issue, share 
split, and reverse share split (consolidation Of shares) that 
have changed the number of equity shares Outstanding, 
without a corresponding change in resources.

Impairment of financial assets
	
In accordance with lnd AS 109, the Company applies 
expected credit loss (ECL) model for measurement and 
recognition of impairment loss on the following financial 
assets and credit risk exposure:
	
a)	
Financial assets that are debt instruments, and 
are measured at amortised cost e.g., loans, 
debt securities, deposits, trade receivables and 
bank balance
	
b)	
Financial assets that are debt instruments and are 
measured as at FVTOCI
	
c)	
Lease receivables under lnd AS 17
	
d)	
Trade receivables or any contractual right to receive 
cash or another financial asset that result from 
transactions that are within the scope of lnd AS 115.
	
e)	
Loan commitments which are not measured as 
at FVTPL
	
f)	
Financial guarantee contracts which are not 
measured as at FVTPL
	
The Company follows ‘simplified approach’ for 
recognition of impairment loss allowance on:
•	 Trade receivables and
•	 Other receivables
	
The application of simplified approach does not 
require the Company to track changes in credit risk. 
Rather, it recognises impairment loss allowance based 
on lifetime ECLs at each reporting date, right from its 
initial recognition.
	
For recognition of impairment loss on other financial 
assets and risk exposure, the Company determines that 
whether there has been a significant increase in the 
credit risk since initial recognition. If credit risk has not 
increased significantly, 12-month ECL is used to provide 
for impairment loss. However, if credit risk has increased 
significantly, lifetime ECL is used. If, in a subsequent 
period, credit quality of the instrument improves such 
that there is no longer a significant increase in credit 
risk since initial recognition, then the entity reverts 
to recognising impairment loss allowance based on 
12-month ECL.
	
Lifetime ECL are the expected credit losses resulting 
from all possible default events over the expected life 
of a financial instrument. The 12-month ECL is a portion 
of the lifetime ECL which results from default events that 
are possible within 12 months after the reporting date.
	
ECL is the difference between all contractual cash flows 
that are due to the Company in accordance with the 
contract and all the cash flows that the entity expects to 
receive (i.e., all cash shortfalls), discounted at the original 
EIR. When estimating the cash flows, an entity is required 
to consider:
•	 All contractual terms of the financial instrument 
(including prepayment, extension, call and similar 
options) over the expected life of the financial 
instrument. However, in rare cases when the expected 
life of the financial instrument cannot be estimated 
reliably, then the entity is required to use the 
remaining contractual term of the financial instrument.
•	 Cash flows from the sale of collateral held or 
other credit enhancements that are integral to the 
contractual terms.
•	 Financial assets measured as at amortised 
cost, contractual revenue receivables and lease 
receivables: ECL is presented as an allowance, i.e., 
as an integral part of the measurement of those 
assets in the balance sheet. The allowance reduces 
the net carrying amount. Until the asset meets write-
off criteria, the Company does not reduce impairment 
allowance from the gross carrying amount.
	
Financial liabilities
	
Initial recognition and measurement
	
Financial liabilities are measured at amortised cost 
using the effective interest method includes loans 
and borrowings, derivatives designated as hedging 
instruments in an effective hedge, trade payables and 
other payables.

3.18	 Hedge Accounting
	
The Company designates certain hedging instruments, 
which include derivatives and non-derivatives in respect 
of foreign currency risk, as cash flow hedges.
	
To qualify for hedge accounting, the hedging relationship 
must meet all of the following requirements:
•	 there is an economic relationship between the 
hedged items and the hedging instruments,
•	 the hedge ratio of the hedging relationship is the 
same as that resulting from the quantity of the hedged 
item that the entity actually hedges and the quantity 
of the hedging instrument that the entity actually uses 
to hedge that quantity of hedged item.
•	 the effect of credit risk does not dominate the value 
changes that result from that economic relationship.
	
At the inception of the hedge relationship, the entity 
documents the relationship between the hedging 
instrument and hedged item, along with its risk 
management objectives and its strategy for undertaking 
various hedge transactions. Furthermore, at the 
inception of the hedge and on an ongoing basis, the 
Company documents whether the hedging instrument is 
highly effective in offsetting changes in fair value or cash 
flows of the hedged item attributable to the hedged risk.
	
Cash flow hedges
	
The Company designates derivative contracts or 
non derivative financial assets / liabilities as hedging 
instruments to mitigate the risk of movement in interest 
rates and foreign exchange rates for foreign exchange 
exposure on highly probable future cash flows 
attributable to a recognised asset or liability or forecast 
cash transactions.
	
When a derivative is designated as a cash flow hedging 
instrument, the effective portion of changes in the 
fair value of the derivative / hedging instruments is 
recognized in the cash flow hedging reserve being part 
of other comprehensive income. The Effective portion 
of cash flow hedges is adjusted to the lower of the 
cumulative gain or loss on the hedging instrument and 
the cumulative change in fair value of the hedged item.
	
Any ineffective portion of changes in the fair value of the 
derivative is recognized immediately in the Statement of 
Profit and Loss.
	
If the hedging relationship no longer meets the criteria 
for hedge accounting, then hedge accounting is 
discontinued prospectively.
	
If the hedging instrument expires or is sold, terminated 
or exercised, the cumulative gain or loss on the hedging 
instrument recognised in cash flow hedging reserve till 
the period the hedge was effective remains in cash flow 
hedging reserve until the underlying transaction occurs. 
The cumulative gain or loss previously recognized 
in the cash flow hedging reserve is transferred to the 
Statement of Profit and Loss upon the occurrence of the 
underlying transaction.
	
For any other cash flow hedges, the amount accumulated 
in OCI is reclassified to profit or loss as reclassification 
adjustment in the same period or periods during which 
the hedged cash flows affect profit or loss.
3.19	 Impairment of non-financial assets
	
Non-financial assets other than inventories, deferred tax 
assets and non-current assets classified as held for sale 
are reviewed at each Balance Sheet date to determine 
whether there is any indication of impairment. If any such 
indication exists, or when annual impairment testing 
for an asset is required, the Corporation estimates the 
asset’s recoverable amount. The recoverable amount 
is the higher of the asset’s or Cash-Generating Unit’s 
(CGU) fair value less costs of disposal and its value in 
use. Recoverable amount is determined for an individual 
asset, unless the asset does not generate cash inflows 
that are largely independent of those from other assets 
or groups of assets.
	
When the carrying amount of an asset or CGU exceeds 
its recoverable amount, the asset is considered impaired 
and is written down to its recoverable amount.
	
In assessing value in use, the estimated future cash 
flows are discounted to their present value using 
a pre-tax discount rate that reflects current market 
assessments of the time value of money and the risks 
specific to the asset. In determining fair value less costs 
of disposal, recent market transactions are taken into 
account. If no such transactions can be identified, an 
appropriate valuation model is used. These calculations 
are corroborated by valuation multiples, quoted share 
prices for publicly traded companies or other available 
fair value indicators.
	
Impairment charges are included in profit or loss, except 
to the extent they reverse gains previously recognised 
in other comprehensive income.

Note 29 : Exceptional Item
a)	
Income from InvITs & Related Assets as per fair value measurement
	
With regulatory changes relating to operations of Infrastructure Investment Trust, coupled with changes in business 
environment and emerging business opportunities, the Company has aligned its business model with respect to its 
investment in IRB Infrastructure Trust, IRB InvIT Fund and related assets (“InvITs & Related Assets”).
	
i)	
Consequently, during the quarter ended December 31, 2024, the Company assessed its eligible investments, 
including interest in joint ventures meeting the required conditions under Ind AS 28, “Investment in Joint ventures 
and Associates”, read with Ind AS 27 “Separate Financial Statements” for measurement at fair value through profit 
and loss account (“FVTPL”). Accordingly, on initial recognition, fair value gain of Rs 47,949.12 million (net of deferred 
tax of Rs 16,126.57 million) has been recognised and presented as ‘Exceptional items’ in the Standalone Statement 
of Profit and Loss.
	
ii)	
Subsequent gain on measurement of these investments at fair value have been recognised and presented as “Gain on 
InvITs & Related Assets as per fair value measurement” under revenue from operations in the Standalone Statement 
of Profit and Loss.
	
iii)	
Dividend / Interest income from InvITs & Related Assets” have been presented separately under revenue from 
operations from the date of initial recognition on account of the above change.
b)	
Employee benefit expense (New Labour Codes)
	
Effective November 21, 2025, the Government of India consolidated 29 existing labour regulations into four Labour 
codes, namely, The Code on Wages, 2019, The Industrial Relations Code, 2020, The Code on Social Security, 2020 and 
the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, collectively referred to as the ‘New Labour Codes’. 
The New Labour Codes has resulted in material increase in provision for employee benefits on account of recognition of 
past service costs. Based on the requirements of New Labour Codes and relevant Accounting Standard, the Company 
has assessed and accounted the estimated incremental impact of ` 106.88 million as Exceptional Item in the standalone 
financial statements for the year ended March 31, 2026. Upon notification of the related Rules to the New Labour Codes 
by the State Government and any further clarification from the Government on other aspects of the New Labour Codes, 
the Company will evaluate and account for additional impact if any, in subsequent periods.

(b) 	 Defined benefit plan
	
The Company has a funded defined benefit gratuity plan. The gratuity plan is governed by the Payment of Gratuity  Act, 
1972 (‘the Gratuity Act’) . Under the Gratuity Act, employee who has completed five years of service is entitled to specific 
benefit. The level of benefits provided depends on the member’s length of service and salary at retirement age.  Every 
employee who has completed five years  or  more of service gets a gratuity on departure at 15 days salary (last drawn 
salary) for each completed year of service as per the provision of the Act. The Gratuity is funded with Life Insurance 
Corporation of India (LIC). The Company contributes in the fund every year as premium on the basis of demand raised 
by LIC. The Gratuity Plan provides a lump-sum payment to vested employees at retirement, death, incapacitation or 
termination of employment, of an amount based on the respective employee’s salary and the tenure of employment 
with the Company. The Company contributes Gratuity liabilities to the IRB Infrastructure Developers Limited Employees 
Group Gratuity Scheme (the Trust). Trustees administer contributions made to the Trusts and contributions are invested 
in a scheme with the LIC as permitted by Indian law.

Note 37 : Financial risk management objectives and policies
The Company’s risk management policies are established to identify and analyse the risks faced by the Company, to set 
appropriate risk limits and controls, and to monitor risks and adherence to limits. Risk management policies and systems are 
reviewed regularly to reflect changes in market conditions and the Company’s activities.
The Board of Directors has overall responsibility for the establishment and oversight of the Company’s risk management framework.
In performing its operating, investing and financing activities, the Company is exposed to the Credit risk, Liquidity risk and 
Market risk.
Market Risk
Market risk is the risk that the fair value of future cash flows of a financial instrument will fluctuate because of changes in market 
prices. Market risk comprises three types of risk: interest  rate risk, currency  risk excluding hedge risk (refer note 48) and 
other price risk, such as equity price risk and commodity risk. Financial instruments affected by market risk include loans and 
borrowings, deposits, FVTOCI investments and derivative financial instruments.
Credit risk
Credit risk is the risk that counterparty will not meet its obligations under a financial instrument or customer contract, leading 
to a financial loss. The Company is exposed to credit risk from its operating activities (primarily trade receivables) and from 
its financing activities, including deposits with banks and financial institutions, foreign exchange transactions and other 
financial instruments.
Financial instruments
Credit  risk from  balances with banks, trade receivables, loans and advances and financial  institutions is managed by the 
Company top management in accordance with the Company’s policy. Investments of surplus  funds are made only with approved 
counterparties and within credit  limits assigned to each counterparty. Counterparty credit  limits  are reviewed by the top 
management on an annual basis, and may be updated  throughout the year subject  to approval of the Company’s board of 
directors. The limits  are set to minimise the concentration of risks and therefore mitigate financial  loss through counterparty’s 
potential failure to make payments.
Investment in Equity shares/units 
The Company has investments in equity shares / units and non-convertible debentures. The settlement of such instruments is 
linked to the completion of the respective underlying projects. Such Financial Assets are not impaired as on the reporting date.
Trade receivables
Concentration of credit risk with respect to trade receivables are high, due to the Company’s customer base being limited. All 
trade receivables are reviewed and assessed for default on a quarterly basis.  Based on  historical experience of collecting 
receivables indicate a low credit risk.

(e)	
Performance obligation
	
The Company undertakes Engineering, Procurement and Construction business. The ongoing contracts with customers 
are for road construction. The type of work in these contracts involve construction, engineering, designing, etc.
	
The Company evaluates whether each contract consists of a single performance obligation or multiple performance 
obligations. Contracts where the Company provides a significant integration service to the customer by combining all 
the goods and services are concluded to have a single performance obligations. Contracts with no significant integration 
service, and where the customer can benefit from each unit on its own, are concluded to have multiple performance 
obligations. In such cases consideration is allocated to each performance obligation, based on standalone selling prices. 
Where the Company enters into multiple contracts with the same customer, the Company evaluates whether the contract 
is to be combined or not by evaluating factors such as commercial objective of the contract, consideration negotiated 
with the customer and whether the individual contracts have single performance obligations or not.
	
The Company recognises contract revenue over time as the performance creates or enhances an asset controlled by the 
customer. For such arrangements revenue is recognised using cost based input methods. Revenue is recognised with 
respect to the stage of completion, which is assessed with reference to the proportion of contract costs incurred for the 
work performed at the balance sheet date relative to the estimated total contract costs.
	
Any costs incurred that do not contribute to satisfying performance obligations are excluded from the Company’s input 
methods of revenue recognition as the amounts are not reflective of our transferring control of the system to the customer. 
Significant judgment is required to evaluate assumptions related to the amount of net contract revenues, including the 
impact of any performance incentives, liquidated damages, and other forms of variable consideration.
	
If estimated incremental costs on any contract, are greater than the net contract revenues, the Company recognizes 
the entire estimated loss in the year the loss becomes known. Variations in contract work, claims, incentive payments 
are included in contract revenue to the extent that may have been agreed with the customer and are capable of being 
reliably measured.
(f)	
Revenue recognition for future related to performance obligations that are unsatisfied (or partially satisfied) :
	
While disclosing the aggregate amount of transaction price yet to be recognised as revenue towards unsatisfied (or 
partially) satisfied performance obligations, along with the board time band for the expected time to recognise those 
revenue, the Company has applied the practical expedient in Ind AS 115.
	
Unsatisfied (or partially satisfied) performance obligations are subject to variability due to several factors such as 
terminations, changes in scope of contracts, periodic revalidations of the estimates, economic factors (changes in tax 
laws etc). The aggregate value of transaction price allocated to unsatisfied (or partially satisfied) performance obligations 
is ` 12,257.98 million (March 31, 2025 : `23,711.38 million) is expected to be recognised as revenue in the next one to 
three years. No consideration from contracts with customers is excluded from the amount mentioned above.
(g)	 Practical expedients:
	
Applying the practical expedient in paragraph 63 of Ind AS 115, the Company does not adjust the promised amount 
of consideration for the effects of a significant financing component if at contract inception it is expected that the year 
between when the entity transfers a promised good or service to a customer and when the customer pays for that good 
or service will be one year or less.

(ii) 	 Hedging activities
	
Foreign Currency Risk
	
The Company is exposed to foreign currency risks as explained in note 37 above. In line with the Risk Management Policy, 
the Company has hedged almost 100% of it’s foreign currency borrowings. To that extent, the Company is not exposed 
to foreign currency risk.
	
All borrowing related hedges are accounted for as cash flow hedges.
	
Interest Rate Risk
	
The Company is not exposed to interest rate risks on fixed rate borrowings as explained in note 37 above.
(iii) 	 Hedge Effectiveness
	
There is an economic relationship between the hedged items and the hedging instruments as the terms of the hedge 
contracts match the terms of hedge items. The Company has established a hedge ratio of 1:1 for the hedging relationships 
as the underlying risk of the foreign exchange are identical to the hedged risk components. To test the hedge effectiveness, 
the Company compares the changes in the fair value of the hedging instruments against the changes in fair value of the 
hedged items attributable to the hedged risks.
(iv) 	 Source of Hedge ineffectiveness
	
In case of foreign currency risk,  the main source of hedge ineffectiveness is the effect of the counterparty and the 
Company’s own credit risk on the fair value of hedge contracts, which is not reflected in the fair value of the hedged items. 
The effect of this is not expected to be material.

T0 = Beginning of time period
t = Specific date falling between T1 and T0

MV(T0) = Market Value at T0
C(t) = Cash inflow, cash outflow on specific date

s company that helps

Chairman and MD’s Message
Dear Stakeholders,
Twenty-eight years ago, IRB set out with a single ambition: to build and 
operate world-class road infrastructure for India. FY 2025-26 is the year 
that ambition came of age. If I were to describe it in one word, it would 
be Transformative – not as a description of a single good year, but as the 
culmination of a strategy conceived, tested and refined over two and a 
half decades.
Our B.E.S.T. strategy – Bid, Execute, Stabilise and Transfer 
– is not a slogan we adopted this year; it is the distilled 
wisdom acquired through years of building, owning and 
operating highways across India. In FY 2025-26, that 
wisdom translated into decisive, tangible value creation 
and firmly established IRB as India’s foremost disciplined 
capital-recycling infrastructure platform – a position we 
set out deliberately to earn, and one that is now genuinely 
difficult to replicate.
It is a matter of real satisfaction that this disciplined 
approach has built one of India’s leading, and the largest, 
highway infrastructure asset platforms. Today, the 
IRB Group commands an asset base of approximately 
`94,000 Cr, up from around `80,000 Cr at the start of the 
year. We operate 28 highway assets across 13 states, 
serving millions of road users every day, with our network 
generating over `1 Cr in toll revenue every hour. This did 
not happen by chance – it is the compounding result of a 
platfo

rm built asset by asset, cycle by cycle, and it reflects 
the resilience, quality and maturity of a portfolio that stands 
without a true peer in the Indian roads sector.
Yet the true measure of our success extends well beyond 
the numbers. Somewhere on a national highway in India at 
this very moment, a truck is moving seamlessly through a 
toll plaza we developed, a family is travelling on a road we 
operate and maintain, and another digital toll transaction 
is being processed across our network. These everyday 
moments, repeated millions of times, are the quiet but 
powerful proof of the role our infrastructure plays in 
connecting India, facilitating commerce and supporting 
the nation’s economic growth – and they are, for IRB, the 
most meaningful validation of everything this platform 
was built to do.
Our B.E.S.T. 
strategy remains 
the cornerstone of 
our value-creation 
philosophy, and 
FY 2025-26 was the 
year it truly proved 
itself as a capability 
that sets IRB apart.
India continues to be one of the world’s fastest-growing 
major economies. Despite geopolitical uncertainties and 
global economic volatility, the resilience of the Indian 
economy continued to drive growth in both passenger 
mobility and freight movement, reflected in healthy traffic 
growth across our portfolio and stronger toll collections, 
particularly in the second half of the year. This performance 
is an affirmation – of the quality of our assets, the resilience 
of our business model, and the conviction with which we 
have built for India’s long-term infrastructure story.
FY 2025-26 marked another year of strong operational 
execution across our tolling portfolio. Our highways today 
serve nearly 1.5 Mn vehicles every day and account for 
close to 10% of India’s total toll collections. Toll revenue 
across IRB and our Private InvIT platform grew by nearly 
13% year-on-year, driven by healthy traffic growth, periodic 
tariff revisions and the addition of new operational assets.
Al

l major projects are now operational. The capex cycle 
is complete. We enter the next phase from a position of 
strength, with future growth driven by operating leverage, 
rising toll collections, InvIT distributions, asset rotation 
and recurring O&M income.
From Builder to Owner-Operator: A Strategic Coming 
of Age
FY 2025-26 was a defining year – the year our strategic 
transformation was truly completed. Over its operating life, 
IRB consciously and deliberately reshaped its identity from 
a contractor: first into a developer that took on construction 
risk and ownership, and now into a Sponsor and Operations 
& Maintenance-led platform, with a sharp focus on capital 
efficiency, recurring cash flows, long-term annuity income 
and sustainable shareholder returns. Few infrastructure 
companies in India have made this full journey – from 
contractor, to developer, to institutional owner-operator – 
and fewer still have done so while continuing to grow the 
underlying portfolio at the pace we have.
This is more than a change in business mix. It is the 
evolution of IRB from a project development company 
into a platform built on creating, owning, operating and 
monetising high-quality road infrastructure assets at 
scale. It strengthens the resilience of our business model, 
sharpens earnings visibility, and positions us to deliver 
consistent, compounding value for every stakeholder who 
has placed their trust in us.
B.E.S.T.: The Engine Behind an Incomparable 
Platform
Our B.E.S.T. strategy remains the cornerstone of our 
value-creation philosophy, and FY 2025-26 was the year 
it truly proved itself as a capability that sets IRB apart. 
This continuous, disciplined rotation of assets – bidding, 
executing, stabilising and transferring — is the engine 
behind our growth: every rupee of equity is made to work 
multiple times over, rather than being committed once and 
held for decades. It is this capital velocity, built and refined 
over years of execution, that ha

s allowed us to construct 
a portfolio whose scale and quality are, today, genuinely 
difficult for others to match.

Our B.E.S.T. Strategy in Action during FY 2025-26:
	
Asset Monetisation: Mature operational assets worth 
`8,436 Cr transferred to the IRB InvIT Fund (Public InvIT)
	
Capital Unlocked: Equity capital of nearly 
`4,905 Cr realised
	
Growth Reinvestment: Private InvIT redeployed capital 
into expanding the portfolio by approx. `14,000 Cr in

We also concluded the transfer of the VM7 (Gandeva–
Ena stretch on the Delhi Mumbai Greenfield Expressway) 
project to the IRB InvIT Fund, receiving ~`510 Cr towards 
equity investment while consolidated debt reduced by 
approximately `700 Cr – further strengthening our liquidity 
and reaffirming the discipline behind every transfer 
we execute.
As we continue to execute this capital allocation and 
value-creation strategy with conviction, we are steadily 
reducing the Company’s consolidated net debt, with a clear 
objective of achieving a net debt-free position over the 
next five years. This deleveraging trajectory will enhance 
our financial resilience, improve cash return on equity, and 
give us the flexibility to pursue the next phase of growth 
from a position of genuine strength.
A Portfolio that Stands Apart
Although overall project award activity remained relatively 
subdued during the year, IRB Infrastructure Trust continued 
to strengthen its portfolio by securing TOT-17 and TOT-18, 
with an aggregate enterprise value of approximately 
`14,000 Cr – well above our typical annual project 
additions. Once again, we demonstrated the execution 
e

xcellence that has become our hallmark: achieving 
financial closure for TOT-17 within a remarkably short span, 
and successfully commencing tolling operations on TOT-
17 and TOT-18 on January 23, 2026 and April 1, 2026, 
respectively. Collections from both assets have been in line 
with our expectations since commencement, reaffirming our 
confidence in their long-term potential. TOT-17 carries, for 
IRB, a particular significance – connecting some of India’s 
most revered pilgrimage and heritage destinations, and 
enabling safer, faster and more efficient travel for millions of 
commuters and devotees.
With every project across our platform now operational, 
IRB has entered a new phase – one defined by earnings 
stability, operating leverage and long-term revenue 
visibility that few of our peers can claim. The resilience of 
our business model rests on a portfolio in which over 99% 
of our assets are fully constructed and operational, toll 
tariffs are contractually linked to inflation, and operations 
and maintenance costs account for only around 15% of 
our total cost base. These structural advantages give 
us predictable cash flows, resilience across economic 
cycles, and a portfolio quality that clearly and durably 
differentiates IRB from conventional construction-led 
infrastructure companies.
O&M: The Rising Pillar
Our Operations & Maintenance platform is emerging as 
one of the strongest pillars of our future earnings visibility. 
Unlike conventional EPC-led models that depend on 
continuous order-book replenishment, our O&M business 
provides long-duration, annuity-style revenues with stable 
margins and predictable cash flows. Our O&M order 
book alone stands at `428 Bn, offering 15 to 20 years of 
long-term visibility with healthy margins. We expect the 
contribution of O&M revenues to keep increasing steadily, 
further improving the quality, stability and sustainability of 
our earnings profile.
ESG, Governance, and Our Communities
At IRB, sustainabil

ity is not a statement – it is a practice 
embedded in every aspect of our operations. Our 
investments in renewable energy solutions, reuse of 
Reclaimed Asphalt Product, eco-engineering techniques 
and low-carbon construction practices underscore this 
commitment, and IRB is rated among the top infrastructure 
companies in India for ESG performance.
Our long-term CSR programmes focus on health, 
education, water conservation and community 
empowerment. Initiatives such as the Sujalam Sufalam 
Schemes reflect our commitment to putting our 
resources to work for social good. We continue to 
maintain robust governance through independent 
boards, comprehensive grievance mechanisms, and ISO 
certifications across quality, environment and occupational 
health (9001, 14001 and 45001).
Pioneering Digital, and Now AI
Innovation has always been integral to IRB’s growth journey. 
We have consistently embraced technology not merely 
to improve efficiency, but to change the way highway 
infrastructure is developed, operated and managed. Over 
the years, IRB has stayed at the forefront of digital adoption 
in the Indian roads sector – we were among the pioneers 
of one of India’s first pilot projects for FASTag-based 
electronic toll collection, and among the first infrastructure 
companies to implement an integrated SAP enterprise 
platform, seamlessly connected with our Toll Management 
System, enabling real-time financial and operational 
reporting across our portfolio.
Today, more than 97% of our toll revenue is collected 
digitally through FASTag, with transactions recorded 
automatically and with no human intervention – 
enhancing operational efficiency, improving transparency, 
strengthening internal controls and delivering a superior 
experience for highway users.
Artificial Intelligence now represents the next frontier of 
this journey. IRB is pleased to share that it has initiated the 
implementation of AI-driven solutions across its Operations 
and Maintenance activ

ities, aimed at enhancing preventive 
maintenance, improving asset monitoring, strengthening 
safety management and enabling more data-driven 
decision-making. While these initiatives are still being 
rolled out, AI, together with advanced analytics and digital 
technologies, is expected to further improve operational 
excellence, enhance customer experience and support 
more efficient lifecycle management of our highway assets 
– adopted, as always, thoughtfully and responsibly, in a 
manner that creates sustainable value for our stakeholders.
Our philosophy remains unchanged: technology is not an 
end in itself – it is an enabler of safer roads, better customer 
service, more efficient operations and stronger long-term 
value creation.
Other Updates
In line with the Company’s Dividend Distribution Policy, we 
declared total dividends of approximately `187 Cr during 
FY 2025-26.
During the year, the Company also received distributions 
of approximately `300 Cr from its two InvIT platforms – a 
clear reflection of the robust and steadily improving cash-
generating ability of our mature operational assets as they 
continue to stabilise and grow.
The Company also completed a 1:1 bonus Issue announced 
during the year, reaffirming our confidence in IRB’s long-
term growth prospects.
The Road Ahead
Following the transfer of three BOT assets from IRB 
Infrastructure Trust and one HAM asset from IRB Infra, the 
Private InvIT has proposed the sale of two BOT highway 
assets, with an enterprise value of approximately `4,605 Cr, 
to the Public InvIT – the B.E.S.T. strategy continuing to do 
exactly what it was built to do. The capital unlocked will be 
redeployed into our next phase of growth.
Building on this momentum, we remain firmly on track to 
expand our road asset portfolio to nearly `1.4 trillion over 
the next three to four years – a target that reflects just how 
far this platform has travelled since IRB’s earliest days as a 
road-building company.
Toll-Operate-Tra

nsfer (TOT) projects will continue to be 
our primary growth driver. With the Government’s road 
monetisation pipeline estimated at approximately `4.4 
trillion over the next four to five years – representing 
annual TOT opportunities of `400–500 Bn – IRB is well 
positioned to capitalise on this sizeable opportunity through 
the very capabilities that define us: an integrated platform, 
disciplined capital allocation, and proven expertise in 
acquiring, operating and monetising toll-road assets at a 
scale few in this industry can match.
Gratitude
On behalf of the Board, I extend my sincere appreciation to 
our shareholders for their continued trust and confidence 
– trust that has made this journey from builder to owner-
operator possible. I also thank the National Highways 
Authority of India, MSRDC, HMDA, UPEIDA, our lending 
institutions, investors, business partners and government 
authorities for their continued support and collaboration.
Most importantly, I express my heartfelt gratitude to every 
member of the IRB family. Their commitment, integrity and 
relentless pursuit of excellence have built, brick by brick 
and highway by highway, the platform we stand on today.
As we look ahead, we remain committed to creating 
sustainable long-term value through disciplined 
capital allocation, operational excellence, prudent risk 
management and the highest standards of corporate 
governance. These principles will continue to guide IRB as 
we build infrastructure that contributes to India’s growth, 
while delivering enduring value for our shareholders.

Priorities that Guide our Ascent
Materiality Assessment
A robust materiality assessment guides how we focus our sustainability efforts and report 
transparently on the issues that matter most to stakeholders and long-term value creation. 
Building on previous assessments, we strengthened our approach in FY 2025-26 to reflect both 
our most significant impacts and the ESG issues that are financially material to the business.
Grounded in GRI 3 and informed by leading ESG 
rating methodologies, SASB, IFRS S1/S2 and SEBI’s 
BRSR framework, our double materiality approach 
evaluates environmental, social and governance 
topics through three lenses: stakeholder concerns, 
impact on enterprise value and impact on the 
broader economy, environment and society. Th

is 
helps us connect stakeholder engagement, risk 
management and strategy, while ensuring that our 
disclosures reflect the ESG factors shaping our 
future performance.
Methodology Evolution and Standards 
Alignment
During FY 2025-26, we further evolved materiality 
from a compliance-led exercise into a strategic 
tool that guides how we allocate time, capital and 
management attention. Our enhanced double 
materiality assessment elevated occupational health 
and safety, climate resilience, governance and ethics, 
human capital and responsible supply chains as key 
issues for stakeholders and future performance.
We continued our practice of peer benchmarking and 
sectoral assessment using the SASB Engineering & 
Construction Services Standard. We also aligned the 
process with GRI 3 Material Topics 2021, GRI Universal 
Standards 2021, IFRS S1/S2 guidance and SEBI’s BRSR 
framework. These references ensure that our topic universe 
reflects both impact materiality under GRI and financial 
materiality as viewed by investors and rating agencies.
The key advancement in our methodology is the integration 
of impacts, risks and opportunities into a dynamic double 
materiality framework. Each topic is assessed across 
three dimensions:
	
Stakeholder concerns
	
Impact on the organisation, covering enterprise value
	
Impact on sustainability, covering the economy, 
environment and people
A topic is considered material when it has significant 
actual or potential impacts on people or the environment, 
or when it could reasonably influence the decisions of 
investors and other providers of capital due to its effect 
on enterprise value. Our matrix brings these perspectives 
together and positions each topic based on its importance 
to stakeholders and to the business.
External Frameworks, ESG Rating Methodologies 
and Peer Benchmarking
To complement the GRI 3 impact lens, we mapped 
our topic universe to leading ESG rating providers and 
sector frameworks.

ESG Rating Met

hodologies

priorities identified by leading ESG rating providers. 
These include health and safety, human capital 
development, labour management, community relations, 
opportunities in clean technology and water, board

business ethics and tax transparency. This helped 
confirm the prominence of governance, safety and 
workforce-related topics in our matrix.

Sector materiality maps and industry driver analysis

useful cross-check for our double materiality positioning 
by assessing both external impact on society and the

3, each potential material topic was

The outcome of this process is a double materiality matrix

d

management framework established.

transparency, accountability, ethics, empowering

This approach encourages employees to not only

Risk Management Process
Risk events are systematically identified, assessed and 
prioritised based on their likelihood of occurrence and 
potential impact on established objectives. Following 
the id

entification of risks, a thorough description is 
provided and identified risks are assessed based on the 
Risk Evaluation Framework to estimate their potential 
impact and likelihood of occurrence. Specific control 
measures are evaluated to mitigate each of the risks. 
The combination of the potential impact of a risk and its 
likelihood is used to determine its intensity and scores 
are calculated to carry out analysis. We conduct a 
comprehensive analysis semi-annually, supplemented 
by selective reviews every quarter, ensuring a robust 
and adaptive assessment process. Using this process 
and in alignment with SEBI LODR, IRB’s ERM framework 
addresses risks under 5 categories of risks.

India’s transition from WPI to Producer Price Index (PPI)
Context
The IRB’s annual horizon scanning exercise identified 
distinct developments in India’s price index framework 
that create unprecedented uncertainty for infrastructure 
concessions whose revenue streams are indexed to 
wholesale price benchmarks. This exercise is supported by 
analysis of regulatory publications from NHAI, the Ministry 
of Commerce and Industry (DPIIT), and MoSPI. These 
developments were reviewed by the IRB’s Finance and 
Risk functions in and formally elevated to the emerging risk 
register on the basis that they represent a structural change 
to the indexation architecture of infrastructure concession 
agreements – a change arising from a reconciliation of 
the linking factor with data published by the Office of the 
Economic Adviser and couldn’t have been anticipated when 
the older concession agreements were finalised.
Price index linkage and the risk of indexation 
underperformance relative to actual cost

inflation have 
long been features of India’s infrastructure concession 
landscape. What elevates the current situation to 
an emerging risk of a different and unprecedented 
character is due to recent and specific development as 
mentioned below.
Recently, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry released 
India’s inaugural Producer Price Index data, marking 
the commencement of a formally announced transition 
from WPI – the benchmark embedded in all major NHAI 
concession agreements for annual toll rate revision – to 
PPI over a five-year horizon. The WPI will be progressively 
discontinued by 2031. The PPI, while methodologically 
superior in its measurement of producer-level price 
dynamics and aligned with international standards including 
IMF recommendations, differs structurally from WPI in its 
basket composition, stage-of-production measurement, 
and treatment of services. The trajectory of PPI relative to 
WPI across commodity cycles is not yet established given 
the absence of a PPI historical time series under the new 
2022-23 base. The Company notes that existing concession 
agreements reference WPI specifically, and the contractual 
and regulatory pathway for rebasing toll indexation to 
PPI is ultimately a policy question for NHAI and MoRTH. 
This introduces an unprecedented period of indexation 
uncertainty that the Company is actively monitoring. 
Mitigation
	
Constructive regulatory engagement 
The Company actively participates in industry 
forums, including representations through relevant 
associations and direct engagement with NHAI 
and MoRTH, to contribute to the development 
of practical and equitable frameworks for the 
WPI-to-PPI transition in concession agreement 
contexts. The Company believes that the 
government’s commitment to a consultative 
approach to major policy transitions provides an 
appropriate pathway for industry concerns to be 
addressed constructively.
	
Concession agreement gap analysis 
The Company notes that it approa

ches this matter 
as a constructive stakeholder in India’s infrastructure 
development ecosystem and is confident that the 
government and NHAI, through their established 
frameworks for concessionaire engagement, will 
develop an equitable and operationally practical 
resolution to the indexation transition. A review 
of all active concession and project agreements 
informs the Company’s legal preparedness without 
prejudging any outcome. 
Potential Business Impact
	
Indexation rebasing creates uncertainty on toll 
rates: For the Company’s BOT and HAM concession 
assets whose toll revision formula references WPI, 
the transition to PPI creates a period uncertainty 
during which the annual escalation is applicable to 
toll rates.
	
Concession agreement gap: The model concession 
agreements doesn’t contain provisions specifically 
governing the scenario of the referenced WPI series 
being discontinued and replaced by an alternative 
index. This creates a contractual gap that will need 
to be addressed – through regulatory guidance, 
concession agreement amendments, circular or any 
other suitable mechanism.

to climate risks undergo rigorous assessment and 
engineering interventions in accordance with Relevant

This governance approach enables IRB to proactively 
address climate-related risks while capitalising on low-carbon 
transition opportunities, particularly in areas such as energy 
efficiency, and sustainable infrastructure development.
Strategy
IRB has defined its short-term (0–5 years), medium-term 
(5–10 years), and long-term (Beyond 10 years) strategy 
after a comprehensive peer benchmarking exercise. These 
time frames form the basis for assessing the materiality of 
climate-related risks and opportunities and are embedded 
into risk reviews, strategic planning, and investment 
decision frameworks.
Based on the IPCC RCP Scenarios and seven NGFS climate 
scenarios, IRB has proactively identified a spectrum of 
transition risks, physical risks, and emerging opportunities 
across its diversified portfolio of businesses-ranging from 
BOT and TOT to HAM and airport operations. These insights 
help shape IRB’s medium- and long-term resilience strategy 
under the framework of the Task Force on Climate-related 
Financial Disclosures (TCFD).
For identifying and assessing physical risks, IRB has 
considered IPCC’s Representative Concentration Pathways 
(RCP), RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5. For transition risks, IRB utilised 
India’s Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), Below 
2°C Scenario, NGFS Current Policy and Net Zero 2050 
Scenarios. We mapped the plausible

business impact of the 
following categories of risks and opportunities:
Physical Risks
Physical risks are a result of short-term catastrophes (acute) 
or long-term variations in climate patterns (chronic). Acute 
physical risks are those that are triggered by a specific event, 
such as extreme weather events like cyclones, storms or 
floods. Whereas longer-term changes in climatic patterns 
(e.g. prolonged higher temperatures) may produce sea level 
rise or chronic heat waves, which are referred to as chronic 
physical hazards.
Transition Risks
Transition risks are enterprise risks that arise as a result of 
societal and economic transformations toward a low carbon, 
more environmentally friendly future. These risks can include 
policy and regulatory and legal risks, technological risks, 
market risks and reputational risks. These areas can vary 
in terms of their type, focus and geographical acceptance, 
which can have a financial implication on our business.

approach ensures climate risk is managed alongside

stakeholder expectations.

assessments and continuous monitoring activities designed 
to ensure the ongoing effectiveness of controls and risk 
mitigation measures.

established requirements.

management processes.

defence approach designed to safeguard corporate

disruption and facilitate timely restoration of critical systems

organisational resilience.

Findings from audit and assurance activities are used to 
strengthen controls, implement corrective actions and 
drive continual improvement of the information security 
framework. This process supports ongoing alignment with 
ISO 27001 requirements, evolving regulatory expectations 
and emerging industry best practices.

Recognising Performance Holistically
We follow a blended performance appraisal methodology 
that combines structured assessment with managerial 
judgement. Instead of applying a uniform forced-
distribution or bell-curve approach, managers evaluate 
performance in the context of roles, responsibilities and 
individual contributions.
The assessment considers business outcomes alongside 
tenure, sustained effort, consistency, initiative, work ethic, 
attitude and alignment with our values. It also recognises 
employees who take ownership, go beyond defined 
responsibilities and strengthen our organisational culture.
This approach enables fairer and more credible 
evaluations while ensuring deserving employees receive 
appropriate recognition. It supports employee motivation, 
strengthens engagement and reinforces our Employee 
Value Proposition by acknowledging the full scope of each 
person’s contribution.

emotional well-being of our people. We plan to expand

ed with Sustainable Development Goal 8, our

Safety is a core organisational value that supports 
operational excellence, workforce well-being and

guides our commitment to incident-free operations. We

safely each day.
We integrate safety performance into our operational 
review framework through defined indicators and targets.

supports an incident-free, environmentally responsible

decision-making and enterprise risk management.
Periodic management reviews, project oversight

continuous improvement measures.

mechanisms help maintain consistent safety standards 
across our workforce and value chain.

Building a Proactive Safety Culture
We believe sustainable safety performance depends on making safety part of

everyday decision-making. We are therefore 
progressing from compliance-led practices towards a proactive, risk-based and behaviour-focused approach that engages 
employees, contractors and leadership teams.
Drawing on leading practices across the global construction and engineering sector, our safety culture is built around three 
interconnected pillars.
Engage
We encourage active participation 
through Safety Committees, 
toolbox talks, site inspections, 
workforce consultations, contractor 
engagement and monthly EHS 
communications. Employees and 
workers are encouraged to identify 
hazards, raise concerns and 
contribute to improvement initiatives.
Educate
Continuous learning is integral 
to our safety culture. Employees, 
contractors and visitors receive 
structured EHS inductions, 
technical training, corporate 
safety programmes and on-the-
job learning.
Empower
We encourage employees and 
contractors to report hazards, 
near misses and unsafe 
conditions without hesitation. 
Structured reporting mechanisms, 
incident investigations and 
leadership engagement enable 
them to contribute actively  
to safer workplaces.
Our proactive safety culture is centred on six strategic 
outcomes:
	
Risk prevention through the systematic identification and 
mitigation of hazards before incidents occur
	
Workforce well-being through safe, healthy and 
supportive workplaces that promote physical, mental and 
emotional well-being
	
Regulatory compliance through adherence to legal 
requirements, client specifications, industry guidelines 
and recognised management system standards
	
Operational excellence through stronger execution, 
operating discipline and business continuity
	
Stakeholder trust through responsible conduct 
and greater confidence among employees, clients, 
regulators, investors and communities
	
Cultural transformation through participation, 
continuous learning and personal ownership of 
safety responsibilities
Employees and workers are expected to

raise concerns 
immediately when they observe unsafe conditions, unsafe 
acts or situations involving imminent risk. Work may be 
paused and escalated through the appropriate supervisory 
and EHS channels until the hazard is assessed and suitable 
controls are implemented.
By enabling employees and contractors to speak up, 
intervene and participate in risk mitigation, we reinforce 
personal accountability and embed safety within 
operational decision-making across all project locations.
Integrated Safety and Risk Controls
Our EHS framework brings together risk management, 
workforce participation, regulatory compliance and 
operational discipline to prevent incidents and strengthen 
safety performance.
We conduct internal and external audits, including 
Integrated Management System audits and client 
assessments, in line with ISO 45001 requirements. Project-
specific Safety Management Plans and Traffic Management 
Plans address operational risks and client expectations. 
Together, these measures reinforce accountability, 
improve workforce engagement and support a resilient 
safety culture.
Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA)
Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment is central 
to our safety approach. It enables us to systematically 
identify, evaluate and control workplace hazards across

❖Noise hazard from plant machinery

egress routes

The Context
Hot mix plants involve high-temperature processes, 
moving equipment and multiple operational hazards. 
Uncontrolled access to these areas can expose 
personnel to serious injury, interfere with equipment 
movement and disrupt operations.
Our Intervention
We implemented a structured barricading system 
around the hot mix plant area to strengthen 
access control and create a safer operating 
environment. The initiative was designed as 
an engineering control under the Hierarchy of 
Controls, addressing risk at source rather than 
relying primarily on individual behaviour or personal 
protective equipment.
Key Measures
	
Robust physical barricades around the

operational area
	
Restricted entry for authorised and 
trained personnel
	
Prominent warning signage communicating 
hazards and safe practices
	
Clear segregation of personnel movement from 
plant operations
	
Defined access points to improve supervision and 
site control
Safety Outcomes
The initiative strengthened access control 
around a critical operational area and reduced 
personnel exposure to moving equipment and 
plant-related hazards. It also improved hazard 
communication, reinforced compliance with site 
safety procedures and supported greater awareness 
of restricted zones.
By separating workforce movement from operational 
activities, the barricading system improved discipline 
around the plant and reduced the potential for 
unauthorised entry and operational interference.
Key Takeaway
Physical barricading provides a preventive 
layer of protection by isolating people from 
hazards at source. This initiative reflects our 
focus on proactive risk management and 
demonstrates how practical engineering 
controls can strengthen safety performance 
across project sites.

Identifying Significant Suppliers
During FY 2025-26, we established a structured 
methodology to identify significant suppliers for 
sustainability assessment and monitoring. In line with the 
SEBI Value Chain Disclosure Framework and Industry 
Standards Forum guidance, suppliers individually 
accounting for 2% or more of procurement expenditure 
were classified as significant.
This process identified 11 significant suppliers, together 
representing approximately 51% of total procurement 
expenditure. The assessment covered publicly available 
information on environmental management, climate 
commitments, occupational health and safety, human rights, 
labour practices, business ethics and governance.
The exercise established a baseline for future engagement 
and enables us to focus on suppliers with the greatest 
business relevance and potential value chain impact.
The assessment focused on publicly available disclosures 
and information relating to environmental management, 
climate commitments, occupational health and safety, 
human ri

ghts, labour practices, business ethics and 
governance systems. The exercise established a baseline 
for future supplier engagement and enhanced visibility of 
sustainability-related risks and opportunities across the 
value chain.
The desktop assessment revealed differing levels of ESG 
disclosure maturity across supplier categories. Suppliers 
operating in regulated sectors such as energy, cement and 
steel generally maintain publicly available sustainability 
disclosures and established ESG management systems. 
In contrast, privately held construction, infrastructure and 
industrial suppliers often exhibit more limited public ESG 
reporting, creating opportunities for future engagement, 
awareness and capability building.
The assessment highlighted differing levels of ESG 
disclosure maturity across supplier categories.
Supplier Assessment Insights
The assessment indicated varying levels of ESG disclosure 
maturity across supplier categories. Suppliers in highly 
regulated sectors, including fuel, energy and cement, 
generally maintained established sustainability governance 
systems, public disclosures and climate commitments.
Construction and infrastructure service providers had 
comparatively limited public ESG disclosures. This may 
reflect lower levels of formal reporting among privately held 
businesses rather than weaker sustainability performance.
Steel suppliers represented approximately 11% of 
procurement expenditure. Of this, around 8% was 
associated with privately held suppliers using a combination 
of Electric Arc Furnace and integrated Direct Reduced Iron 
production routes. These pathways have different energy 
and emissions profiles and provide useful insights into the 
environmental characteristics of key construction materials.
A significant share of assessed procurement expenditure 
was also linked to suppliers with investment-grade financial 
profiles, supporting supply chain resilience and business 
continuity. The assessment did not ident

ify any significant 
supplier requiring a formal corrective action plan or 
termination of the relationship.

commitments to environmental protection, pollution 
prevention, resource conservation and continual 
performance improvement. It defines responsibilities and 
objectives across functions and provides the foundation 
for integrating environmental considerations into 
our operations.
We have implemented an Environmental Management 
System aligned with ISO 14001:2015. It provides a 
structured framework for identifying, assessing, monitoring 
and mitigating environmental aspects and risks. Embedded 
within our day-to-day operations, the system supports 
regulatory compliance, efficient resource utilisation, impact 
reduction and continual improvement. It also strengthens 
sustainable decision-making across the organ

isation.
Sustainability Roadmap
IRB’s long-term sustainability strategy is comprehensively 
represented in our Sustainability Strategy Map, which 
aligns our operational priorities. A central component of this 
strategy is our commitment to achieving net-zero carbon 
emissions. We are actively pursuing this goal through a 
range of practical initiatives, including transitioning to 
renewable energy sources, enhancing energy efficiency, 
and implementing low-carbon technologies across our 
projects and electrification efforts. 
Operational Initiatives and Continuous Improvement
Our renewable energy assets generated 3.34 Mn kWh 
of electricity during the year. We also increased the use 
of electrically powered operations, resulting in direct 
cost savings and lower dependence on diesel. At project 
sites with reliable grid connectivity, the use of electricity 
for bitumen heating can generate further savings while 
supporting cleaner and more energy-efficient construction.
We plan to replace Thermia-heated bitumen tanks with 
electrically heated tanks, further reducing fuel consumption 
and improving operational efficiency.
We have also optimised resource deployment by using a 
single mobile plant across multiple projects within a cluster 
rather than installing separate plants for each project. This 
model improves equipment utilisation, lowers capital and 
operating costs, simplifies logistics and promotes more 
efficient resource use.
We continued to integrate Reclaimed Asphalt Pavement 
(RAP) technology into our existing facilities. Advanced 
RAP processing equipment enables asphalt materials to 
be recycled and reused, reducing waste and dependence 
on virgin materials. The technology also supports energy 
conservation while allowing us to produce high-quality 
asphalt mixes. Its continued deployment strengthens 
our approach to sustainable and resource-efficient 
road construction.
We invested in next-generation construction equipment 
compliant with BS-VI emiss

ion norms. These additions 
helped reduce exhaust emissions, improve fuel efficiency 
and strengthen operational performance. We also 
expanded LED-based street lighting and solar-powered 
infrastructure across our operations and maintenance 
portfolio, supporting long-term energy conservation.
Our procurement practices increasingly favour sustainable 
alternatives to conventional construction materials. These 
include Ground Granulated Blast Furnace Slag (GGBS), 
Glass Fibre Reinforced Polymer (GFRP), Manufactured Sand 
(M-sand) and Crumb Rubber Modified Bitumen (CRMB). 
Their use supports environmental compliance, resource 
efficiency, innovation and the development of more climate-
resilient infrastructure.
Energy Efficiency and GHG Emissions
Efficient energy management is central to our sustainability 
objectives and operational performance. Our approach 
focuses on reducing fuel-based energy consumption, 
increasing electrification and integrating cleaner energy 
sources across operations.
We quantify greenhouse gas emissions in accordance with 
the GHG Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting 
Standard. Our assessment covers carbon dioxide equivalent 
emissions and follows the operational control approach. 
Details of the emission factors and Global Warming 
Potentials used are provided in Annexure 1 on Page 146.
Diesel and other fuels continued to account for a significant 
share of our energy consumption, primarily due to the 
operation of construction equipment, diesel generators 
and transportation vehicles. At the same time, the share 
of electricity, including renewable electricity, increased 
as we upgraded infrastructure and adopted lower-carbon 
technologies. We regularly monitor energy consumption 
across operations to identify efficiency opportunities and 
reduce wastage.

Water Circularity 
We continued to implement water conservation and 
circularity measures across our operations. Treated 
wastewater from Sewage Treatment Plants and 
sedimentation systems was reused for non-potable 
applications wherever feasible. Water-efficient curing 
methods, including spray systems and curing compounds, 
helped reduce freshwater use. Potable water was not used 
for dust suppression.
Beyond our project boundaries, we supported groundwater 
recharge and community water resilience through the 
Sujalam Sufalam Jal Abhiyan. Under the programme, water 
conservation structures with a cumulative storage capacity 
of 53,427 Cum. were developed, benefiting more than 4,700 
people across two villages. 
Water Stewardship 
We recognise water as a critical natural resource and 
manage it responsibly across the lifecycle of our highway 
and expressway projects.
During FY 2025-26, our total water withdrawal was 2.64 Mn 
KL, of which 2.34 Mn KL was consumed across operations. 
The increase was primarily driven by the expansion of our 
project portfolio and the progression of HAM and BOT 
projects into water-intensive construction stages.
Water was mainly used for concrete batching and curing, 
subgrade and pavement compaction, dust suppression, 
roadside plantation and workforce welfare facilities at 
project sites.

Protecting Bridge Foundations. Preserving River Ecosystems.
#Case Study
TechRevetment Bridge Abutment Protection at 
the Ganga, Ambika and Mindhola Rivers
Bridge abutments located along active river systems 
face continued exposure to erosion, changing water 
flows and soil movement. Protecting these structures 
requires a solution that strengthens infrastructure 
resilience while limiting disturbance to surrounding 
river habitats.
Under VM7 Expressway Private Limited, Geoquest 
India Pvt. Ltd. implemented the TechRevetment 
system at the Ambika River Bridge at km 192+653 
and the Mindhola River Bridge at km 214+554. 
The interventio

n formed part of the National 
Highways Authority of India’s infrastructure 
enhancement programme.
The Intervention
TechRevetment provides the strength and durability of 
concrete slope protection without the complex, time-
intensive installation associated with conventionally 
formed concrete paving.
The system used non-woven geotextiles, geotextile 
fabrics and fine aggregate concrete to protect 
the bridge abutments and stabilise the adjoining 
riverbanks. Its flexible structure allowed it to adapt to 
the natural contours of the bank slopes and channel 
beds, improving coverage while reducing the need for 
extensive ground alteration.
Installation involved precise site grading and the 
controlled placement of underwater panels by trained 
divers. These methods helped minimise disturbance 
to river habitats while creating a durable protective 
layer around the bridge foundations.
Environmental Benefits
By stabilising the riverbanks, the system helps 
prevent erosion, reduce downstream sedimentation 
and protect aquatic ecosystems. Compared with 
conventional riprap or concrete-block solutions, its 
optimised material design also lowers resource use 
and the environmental footprint of installation.
Panel sizing, material planning and on-site quality 
controls further reduced construction waste and 
supported more efficient use of concrete and 
geotextile materials.
Safety and Capability Building
The project was executed through defined safety 
protocols covering manual handling, electrical work 
and underwater operations. Mandatory personal 
protective equipment and risk-based controls were 
applied to protect employees and specialist workers.
Training was provided to equipment operators, 
divers and site supervisors, strengthening 
local capabilities in advanced geotechnical and 
underwater construction techniques.
Quality and Governance
Materials and concrete were subjected to rigorous 
testing in line with applicable ASTM, IRC and Indian 
Standards. Detailed c

onstruction methodologies and 
quality assurance plans were submitted to the client 
and consultant for review and approval.
Environmental risk assessments were also 
conducted before and during execution to ensure  
compliance and prevent avoidable ecological  
disturbance.
Creating Lasting Value
The intervention strengthens the long-term stability 
of the Ambika and Mindhola river bridges while 
supporting safer and more reliable connectivity 
for surrounding communities. By combining 
resilient engineering, efficient material use, 
ecological protection and disciplined execution, 
the project demonstrates how infrastructure can be 
strengthened while respecting the natural systems 
around it.
Biodiversity and Ecological Integration
We integrate biodiversity considerations throughout 
the planning, design, construction and maintenance of 
our highway and expressway projects. This approach 
helps minimise ecological impacts and strengthen 
ecosystem resilience.
We continued to adopt nature-based engineering solutions 
to improve environmental performance and infrastructure 
resilience. These included coir-based geomats, vetiver 
grass, erosion-control blankets, hydroseeding, mulching, 
geotextiles, composite mats and stone-pitched nallah 
diversions. Together, these measures helped stabilise 
slopes, control erosion, conserve natural drainage and 
protect topsoil.
